What's there to say that hasn't been said yet? I think Act 2 of Hiveswap is phenomenal. It takes the game in a different direction, whereas Act 1 has mostly focused on locations, items and descriptions, Act 2 knocks it out of the park by focusing on what we all really wanted from the game. Trolls. And lots of them!

I think it's by no means an exaggeration when I say that what Act 2 puts into form is something every Homestuck fan has been wanting to see from day 1. More Trolls, more interactions. The train is a fantastic setting as well, allowing the player a highspeed hemospectrum tour that openly displays what has been canonically known for a long time, the way trolls interact with each other according to their social hierarchy dictated by blood.

And do not get me started on the music. While Act 1 had catchy tunes, Act 2 really knocked it out of the park with some absolute bangers (Quadrant Confusion) and some actually terrifying jams (Down with the Clown).

Overall, this is what we've been waiting for. All those years in the making, what Act 1 failed to deliver was realized in Act 2 and I'm very happy for it. It bodes well for future acts and it has me genuinely excited to see what's bound to come in the next 4 years.

The good:
Excellent writing, characters and world-building overall.
Relatively appealing protagonists.
Excellent, detailed visual aesthetic. Special mention to the manga-style portrait switch in the trial scene.
Touches on meaningful themes of class and gender.

The meh:
More challenging then the first, and not always in the best way. Perhaps I was impatient, but I felt the need to use a walkthrough to help out in certain points, whereas I was able to figure most everything out in the first episode. But the hardcore among us will most likely appreciate this.
Snowpiercer 'homage' works well in the story, but borders on plagiarism.
A bit too much back-tracking required toward the end.

The bad:
The Phoenix Wright-esque trial scene was a huge hurdle to overcome for me. For most of the game a little luck and trial and error will get you through. But this section required you to take notes and trial and error would often result in an End Game. I almost gave up here, and would have if a walkthrough hadn't been available online to help out.
The story ends on a kind of cliffhanger, which is a bit of a downer.

Verdict:
It's got it's flaws and its short (I finished in just under 6 hours), but push comes to shove, this was a worthy sequel to Act 1, and I'm interested in seeing where the story goes from here.

I would like to start by saying I loved this game.  Why?  It continued a story I am invested in, has great art, wonderful music, and the characters are funny and enjoyable to learn about.  If you don't like to struggle at a puzzle for more than a few minutes and want to just push forward, this game may initially (especially based on other reviews) seem to be entirely not for you.  I would entirely agree with that, if it were not for the detailed and helpful hints that the game provides for you that makes any frustration go away, and gives way to more fun character interactions, and new "people" to interact with!  

Do I think that Act 1 is better?  In some ways, yes, in others no.  Act 1 admittedly looked much better, the cutscenes and animation were much more fluid, and were some of the best parts of the game.  If that's all that you loved about Hiveswap, maybe this isn't for you; however, if you enjoy fun characters and played Act 1, I would say that it definitely is for you.

Pros:
Great art and character designs.
Fun interactions between characters I know, and ones that I just met.
Continues a story that I am still invested in.
Music slaps.
It costs $15 (normal price) for an enjoyable 6 hour experience, with achievements to go back for if so inclined.

Cons:
Animation is not as good as Act 1.
The development history and lengthy amount of time since Act 1.
Some bugs here and there, most were resolved by reloading a save.
[spoiler]The Trial portion went on a bit longer than I would have liked, but it was still enjoyable.[/spoiler]

Spoilery bits
[spoiler]Overall, I enjoyed the experience.  The clown car was genuinely fear inducing, and the killing of a purple-blood troll was not something I expected from Hiveswap if I am being honest.  I went in expecting less than I got, and left it wanting to play Act 3 when ( or if) it comes out.  Do I see myself replaying this game?  Probably not, but I do not normally replay story games. [/spoiler]

TL;DR
If you liked Act 1 for nothing but the animation and cutscenes, this isn't for you.  If you liked the characters, and the story, I would say it definitely is for you. [b]Most important thing to note, is that if you get stuck, use the hints.  They are really good at getting you on the right track, and make the game so much more enjoyable[/b]

I have a very mixed view on ACT 2. I think some of the gameplay was annoyingly tedious, especially the last train car. Having to go back and forth through the train cart on fetch quests (which the game even acknowledges) is fucking boring. On the flip side, I felt the trial section was really fucking fun to play. This game does struggle with the issue of throwing ALOT of characters at you, and I will not lie, I struggled to remember everyone's names. However, I also loved most of these characters, despite struggling to remember names. Nobody was truly forgettable, as one-dimensional as some of them were. The music is wonderful as is to be expected, and I love the art, although there are some issues with the art. For example, characters don't seem to have many if any proper transitions between animations while being talked to, which is very off-putting and I am not sure why this was let through. Another issue I have is the blatant lack of properly animated cutscenes, most the cutscenes in this one are instead slideshows at best, with few animations spread here and there. It feels like they put less effort into this one compared to the bang of love that ACT 1 had poured into it. The UI also has been changed, and I can't say I'm a fan of the way the textboxes look, although that is largely subjective.

The story was pretty fun, as is to be expected, and I genuinely felt hooked on finishing this game (ended up playing it all in one sitting). The writing does feel a little blander, however, especially with the flavour dialogue. 

I will also take a moment to complain about the way they've gone about releasing Hiveswap. The episodic formula is not working. There is far too much time between episodes. That being said, I don't want them to try to rush the acts out, because that'll only make things worse. [b]To preface this[/b] - I am not a die-hard Homestuck fan. Pretty far from it, really. I am primarily writing this as a fan of point and click adventure games and this review is mostly for people who are fans of point and click adventure games. I read it, sure, but it's not my typical cup of tea. On a very surface level I enjoyed acts 1-5 and I kind of tapped out at act 6 due to a variety of smaller issues that began to compound into a singularly hair-pulling reading experience, only finishing it out of some nebulous sense of obligation due to the amount of time sunk into reading it. I enjoyed it, didn't love it, but I very much appreciate its existence and I think its better qualities far outweigh its negatives. Nevertheless, this is not a review of Homestuck.

Hiveswap, in a meta sense, is an inherently fraught topic that - without getting into the layers-upon-layers of internal drama, semi-failed promises, and general mishandling of the overall IP after its acquisition - I'll just say is complicated from essentially any standpoint that is not the structural content of the actual game. Said content, however, is pretty simple.

Hiveswap (as a whole) is a very classic point and click adventure game in the same vein as something like Pajama Sam or Day of the Tentacle. It is also a very *good* point and click adventure game. The presentation is clean and vibrant. Flavortext is abundant and high quality, with essentially every item in your inventory having some form of interaction with whatever new thing or person you haplessly try throw it at to see if you missed anything important. While there aren't necessarily different routes, there are branching paths that have some subtle yet tangible effects on dialogue and the options available to you for puzzles, which - again, while mostly an underscore - is a welcome addition that makes replays to see all the writing an appealing option for after the credits roll. I especially appreciate the fact that almost every "puzzle" in the game has more than one solution available, and the game doesn't necessarily railroad (pun maybe intended? subconciously?) you into whichever you stumble upon first. I cannot overstate how well this game and its predecessor/first chapter function as point and click games - I'd list them as must-plays for anyone who appreciates the genre. 

When discussing the pacing of the game it's important to understand the basic conceit when it comes to its structure. The game is segmented and split into train cars, which function as self-contained vignettes containing their own subplot and puzzle before moving onto the next one. In total, if you count the brief time spent before getting on the train, there are 6 of these. While an even split of time between all of them shouldn't necessarily be expected as some sort of design requirement, when each of these mini-chapters are based primarily around their respective "gimmicks" when it comes to the characters and overall themes + aesthetics being explored therein, it stands to reason that given the character-driven (both the literal characters as well as the more chimerical character of the area) nature of the game, that it would be generally somewhat [i]*bad*[/i] to not evenly pace the amount of time spent in each. Unfortunately, this somewhat bad thing is exactly what the game does. I am not going to say exactly which are which, but there is one train car that gets skipped over almost immediately, one that takes up a solid 1/3 to 1/2 of the runtime of the game, and one that barely has you interact with the car at all, mostly asking you to go back and talk to people you've already thoroughly talked to. It's not game ruining, sure, but what really gets my goat about this whole thing is that I never once got the impression that any of these cars had more or less to say than the others. They all are pretty much matched in potential, which leads to a lopsided experience where you can tell some parts have aspects left untapped while others would have served much better as more succinct experiences.

Are these issues game ruining? Nah. But they are frustrating in a very strange and kind of ephemeral way to the point where I couldn't put my finger on it until I was thinking in retrospect. Anyways.

I won't comment much on the more Homestuck-y and "cringe" aspects of the writing, as well as its departures from previous things within the franchise. For a few reasons. Mostly: I don't really care. Secondarily: A lot of what I'd say has been said verbatim previously by people with far more stake in this whole thing than me. Yeah, its a little tryhard at times when it comes to the general vulgarity of it all. There's some scant use of modern internet terminology that doesn't fit the overall vibe. The troll blood castes and their populations are victim to a pretty severe case of Flanderization and are frankly just a little [i]*off*.[/i] None of these things should really concern you if you aren't invested in the sanctity of the Homestuck name though, for most normal people any of the above gipes will probably amount to a vaguely miffed eye-roll, a fleeting yet disapproving squint, or - more likely - nothing at all. 

Outside of these frankly small personal issues, the writing is very good - especially for flavortext and interactions between our two main characters. It's not Shakespearean, but it is strikingly natural at times and the sense of humor in the flavortext can catch you off guard with some very honest laughs pretty consistently. The narrative manages to make the story feel prescient at most points during the game despite the overall structure essentially being a series of very, very tangential diversions. The player is ostensibly expected to try and find all the text and dialogue possible, taking them farther and farther away from the primary goal in the process, so it is an impressive feat to be able to still keep someone invested in and not forgetful of said goal throughout the whole runtime.

I'm not terribly qualified to speak on the visuals, art has never been my thing, and getting into them will invariably drag me into speaking on the more meta aspects of this game's development and all that jazz, so I'll keep it brief. It doesn't look as good as act 1 which can be theorized to be because it had overall less people working on it and a somehow more rocky development cycle than the first chapter. Irregardless of this, the game looks great - the first act is a very, very high bar to clear. Environments universally are great and the stark contrast between them is very well executed and obviously thematically relevant. The visuals paired with the soundtrack and audio design impart such a pointed sense of individuality in every section that the player is almost immediately able to ascertain a whole suite of traits regarding each group of characters and each train car. It's done so well that it can sometimes come off as hammy, or too in-your-face about the points it wants to make. However: the alien world the game takes place on is simply very in-your-face by nature, and I personally believe that a more subtle approach would be ill-suited to the setting. 

If you like point and click games, play it. If you like Homestuck, play it and also maybe don't be so stuck up about it? 

That's really all I have to say. On the matter.

A really excellent game that expands on Act 1 in a really satisfying way. It has some rough edges (as seems inevitable for a project this ambitious made by such a small team, and that's without considering any of the complications that likely went down during this game's, to put it charitably, rather extended development cycle), but on the whole it merges the more traditional adventure game charm of Act 1 with much more focus on dialogue and world-building to great effect. That said, it isn't without some more avoidable problems.

Notably, as some other reviewers have noted, the Ace Attorney parody / homage segment has some significant problems with the puzzle design. It's too long and involved to get away with the rather low level of polish on the gameplay, and in some ways it feels as if the writers desire to fully explore the scenario is highly mismatched with the level of effort the designers wanted / were able to put into it. That said, for me personally it was one of the highlights of the story, and I would be interested in seeing What Pumpkin do something else in that style in the future (though preferably not as a detour to an entirely different type of game). Other problems include some notable bugs (some of which are already patched out at the time of writing) and general puzzle design issues of lesser significance than the trial segment, but nothing particularly irritating given the in-game hint system.

On the unambiguously positive side, the writing is almost all phenomenal. While it is somewhat less charming than the playful tone of Act 1, there's still plenty of fun to be had even as the game begins to get into significantly darker territory. There were multiple points toward the end of the Act that were real gut-punches that I'm still thinking about now, and the game's themes coalesce wonderfully as it goes on. Some of the side characters come off as overly one-note, something that particularly stood out for the many which were already shown as more fully developed in the Friendship Simulator spin-off, but given the limited role most of them play here that's understandable so long as future installments better showcase and advance the complexity they have already been shown to have in said spin-off. That said, several characters who didn't quite click for me in FriendSim became compelling here, so it goes both ways.

On the whole it's an extremely fun ride, and despite some significant bumps it improved on its predecessor in almost every way. Additions like paths that diverge in actually meaningful ways and the greater synergy between the story and gameplay elements consistently adds to the already stellar writing. I for one can't wait to see what happens next.

Hiveswap Act 2 has been in the pipes for a long time, not quite the wait for the original game but certainly enough to get some expectations going. Overall the game delivers the goods narratively on most fronts, while I was a little sad the plot wasn't pushed forward to the point of encountering any brand new characters - the further development of Joey and Xefros both invididually and as a duo helps make up for that substantially.

Hiveswap Act 2's greatest strength in my opinion would be it's character writing, it introduces almost the entire cast of the Friendsim spin off game to bounce off both each other and our protagonists in interesting and dynamic ways. The framing device for doing so, Joey and Xefros boarding a train segregated by blood based social caste and navigating from bottom to top of the social heirarchy is clever and allows distinct levels with their own themes to be presented. Because of this even relatively minor characters feel fully realised and often offer interesting commentary on Alternia as a planet, in particular I adored the Jadeblood cloister - where mum friend Bronya desperately tries to keep a group of people who absolutely hate eachother together. But it's obvious that the strongest members of the game's cast are it's main duo, radical lawyer Tyzias, punk Elwurd  and eccletic clown rapper Marvus, and the game does well to centralise them. The development of the main duo in particular feels realistic and grounded, offering some pathos and grounding to a story that might otherwise feel a bit too silly.

As well while it's hard to particularly get into comedy in a review without just quoting jokes, the writing for the game is witty, clever and has a strong sense of both creating comedy from the premise of Alternia as a planet of wayward teens and character dynamics. 

Art wise while there isn't quite the sense of atmosphere as offered by the Harley manor for much of the game, this is made up for by an incredibly strongly designed cast - including dense collages of background trolls in the lowblood carriages. However I felt there was a noticeable uptick in the background spectacle as the game went on, especially in the final two levels. Additionally Hiveswap for areas where typical adventure game asthetics won't quite convey a scene, will use some incredibly charming animatics and short animations to get itself across. Leading to some of the most comedic and in some cases, tense moments in the game.

Music wise as expected from a WhatPumpkin project it's nothing but bops top to bottom. In particular I loved the trains theme being played with different styles from carriage to carriage, again helping convey instantly a sense of what each caste is like at a glance.

The main area of critique for me is while the game is excellent at conveying character and location, I found it more lacking when trying to convey gameplay. In particular while the tealblood cart presents a fun homage and interesting commentary on Alternian law - I found it mostly fustrating trying to navigate the puzzles here and decided to just use a walkthrough to better enjoy the scene. It's a shame as I do genuinely admire the efforts to push the gameplay depth from Act 1's very sparse offerings but I feel this is perhaps a less strong area for the team - having previously delivered games that are more interactive narratives. The bee dance section was a fun distraction though, and minigames similar to that feel like a natural fit for the series. 

In conclusion despite the anticipation Hiveswap Act 2 delivered the goods, offering the sharp, insightful and clever writing I've come to expect from the WhatPumpkin team, and I am eagerly awaiting the next chapter of Joey and Xefros' journey.

[h1]It's Hard Being an Adventure Game. It's Hard, and Nobody Understands[/h1]

I find [i]Hiveswap: Act 2[/i] to be a particularly difficult game to review. If you backed this game on kickstarter nearly a decade ago and played through Act 1, then sure, it's worth sinking a few hours into, I recommend it. But if not, if you're a fan of narrative storytelling, if you're a fan of adventure games, heck, even if you're a [i]~Homestuck Fan~[/i] then, eeehhh.. It's still not such an easy recommendation.

The game's got problems.

Don't get me wrong, the art is beautiful, the soundtrack has got some [i]major[/i] bangers (already threw some into my exercise playlist, what's good), even the animation is pretty nice. Sure, the animation is choppy and a little rough, but it's got a sort of old-shcool point-and-click adventure game charm to it that really works. The visual and audio aspect of the game is great, no problems there; like, for real, look up the anime sprites and the song from the conductors cabin and you'll have a pretty good idea of the weight this game can pull artistically. In terms of narrative, character, pacing, and gameplay though? Oofy doofy, that's a tough one.

We have to get into big time spoiler territory here, folks. Suffice to say the puzzles and gameplay are [i]by far[/i] the weakest aspects of this game. You may as well be reading a Young Adult novel about Alternia.

[b]##BIG FAT SPOILERS ABOUT BASICALLY ALL ASPECTS OF THE GAME BELOW##[/b]

Maybe this one is on me, maybe it's because I played [i]Hiveswap: Act 1[/i] four years ago, but the opening to this game felt very jarring to me. We're told that our objective is to go to a party we previously never heard of (Jeevik Week) to meet somebody we've previously never heard of (Cridea Jeevik) so that we can... Help the rebellion? Get Joey back to Earth? It's all very vague, though I suppose Joey isn't [i]supposed[/i] to have clear information at this point. Of course, we have to actually [i]get[/i] to Jeevik Island, but before that we have to get to the train that will get us to Jeevik Island. 

And this is probably the weakest point of the game, the opening act. The motivation is thin, the setting feels contrived, and it sets the tone for all the puzzles and progression going forward. That is to say, it all feels very [i]railroaded[/i], and this is before boarding a literal linear train! From the start of the game, the progression follows a simple path of moving from the left screen to the right screen and finding the single item or talking to the single person necessary to progress; there is very little problem solving or thinking involved. A sharp microcosm of this issue can be seen in the bee farm (apparently owned by a fella named [i]Zebede[/i]? Idk, I didn't play [i]Friendsim[/i]); this environment features all sorts of elements: beehives, fruit plants, a windmill, a mind-honey well, a fruit press, even a hive interior! Plenty of pieces to get the gears turning, just begging to be used in some sort of weird and intricate puzzle! So how do you clear this screen? You knock a book off a shelf and learn a skill you literally never use in the game ever again. Amazing. 

This really is my major critique of the game. There is no exploration, no problem solving, no gameplay. It really is just moving from left to right, encountering a (usually highly contrived) obstacle, and finding the single person to talk to to clear it. The world is interesting enough, and it's very fun to see Alternia outside the context of Homestuck, with tons and tons of unique trolls to meet, and even to examine the finer points of Alternian society and the consequences of the Hemospectrum casting system (even if Xefros very blatantly explains the real-world parallel and moral at the end), but this narrative could have just as easily been told in a short story; it doesn't [i]feel[/i] like an adventure game, it doesn't feel like this game's status as a video game actually [i]does[/i] anything for it. Anyway, once you actually get past the opening to the game and onto the train, I actually feel like things pick up a little bit. In lieu of writing out my bloviated thoughts on the rest of the game, here's a power ranking of each of the train cars:

 - Rust/Bronze Car [4/6] - Literally all of the points for this car come from the music and the fantastic visuals. Seeing dozens of unique trolls full of personality crammed into a dingy car is just great. The puzzle here is boring and sucks.

- Gold/Olive Car [2/6] - Conflict is weak, puzzles are weaker. I literally cleared the strife on my first try, I didn't even know what was going on. Suppose this car gave Xefros an opportunity to drop an explanation of Troll quadrants that's too trite for Homestuck veterans and probably too vague/confusing for Homestuck neophytes
 
- Jade/Teal Car [5/6] - Oh this is where the game went! Maybe they actually put [i]too much[/i] problem solving into this one, because boy is the trial long and convoluted! Though as an [i]Ace Attorney[/i] fan, I actually quite enjoyed this car, and found myself with a weird affection for everyone involved in the trial by the end

- Blue/Indigo [1/6] - Look, the most contrived puzzle so far! And we get to do it three times? And the music and visuals aren't nearly as fun as any other car? I think I'd like that cute blue blood to gouge my eyes out after all ::::)

- Purple [3/6] - The obstacle for this car is actually pretty good, the reveal is dramatic, and the characters are fun but... Of course the puzzle is solved with backtracking and talking, no [i]actual[/i] creative problem solving. The resolution is genuinely pretty surprising though, which is cool!

- Violet/Fuchsia [6/6] - Yes!! Here it is! Point-and-click adventure video games! We did it, we made it! We get to use items on stuff and solve a weird and intricate puzzle! Oh, and the music kicks absolute [i]major ass[/i]? I don't even [i]care[/i] that the puzzle is kinda janky and hard to follow at times (why couldn't I use telekinesis on the lever at the end?), it doesn't matter!

So, yeah, I enjoyed my time with [i]Hiveswap: Act 2[/i], for sure. The download code got dropped into my email inbox, so it was worth spending nearly eight hours with (I'm a slow reader, get off my back). The writing feels sloppy and confused, and many of the UX aspects felt unpolished, but the game's get enough going for it that- Oh my [i]gosh[/i] I just remembered-

But the Homestuck writing charm was there, and that carries the experience. Homestuck opens by leaning hard on a bunch of data structure jokes that 90% of the audience is just confused by, it's only fitting that a Homestuck game leans hard on a genre crossover that's going to confuse a large chunk of the audience.

The thing that leaves me really happy with this game and excited for the next chapter is that the sense of tension and suspense is really well handled - the stakes ratchet in a way that doesn't feel forced and has enough valleys to create some salient character moments.

In a lot of ways, Hiveswap Act 2 reminds me of the best parts of Hivebent - if that was one of your favorite parts of Homestuck, you'll probably like this game a lot.

I was looking forward to this after being kinda concerned it would never be, and based on my enjoyment of the first part, this one did not disappoint. Classic point and click adventure with the worst possible part being a puzzle or two that can be a bit difficult to figure out exactly what the game wants you to do. I had heard of some possible buggy parts, but did not encounter any on my playthrough so I can't say for certain what the deal is behind those.

Definitely a high point is the richness of the setting while simultaneously not requiring you to know the super dense lore from Homestuck to get into. The bite sized approach is as appreciated this time as it was last time. Characters are generally quirky, fun, well designed, and generally memorable. That even random background characters have unique designs is an especially nice touch.

On the downside, I do feel that [spoiler]the trial sequence dragged on quite a bit and could be frequently unintuitive to solve all for an overly long Phoenix Wright parody. I feel that section was disproportionately lengthy compared to the other sections and not quite as entertaining due to the gameplay deviation, though admittedly, I've always found trial sequences in video games rather tedious.[/spoiler] It did create a feeling that the other sections might be underdeveloped or rushed in comparison, though I did still enjoy them.

Also, the choice in music track for one particular section [spoiler]the gold/olive car[/spoiler] had a classic 8 bit sound that got kinda annoying to hear on loop given how long I spent in that particular area.

I do hope Hiveswap is able to fully complete it's story and while I understand that game development is a complicated matter, it would be nice to not have to wait several more years for parts 3 and 4 given how relatively short these are.

Edit: Given the length of time that's passed, it would be nice if nothing else if there was some kind of update or disclaimer so people know what they're getting into. It's been years and while Hiveswap isn't cancelled per se, I would definitely caution getting invested without more substantial and official proof of continued development. Personally, random youtube videos and rumors on social media don't cut it for me. If development is continuing, something more official posted here on Steam would be a big reassurance.

   Initially the starting screen gives you a hit of nostalgia from the first game, tailored with a moving background and music which is heavily reminiscent of the first installment. (Clip) “Ohhh that music...what happens if i click recap”  (do meme where it plays my first video)
   Act 2 starts out from the end of the first game, where Joey and Xefros are riding on the deer cat, so it's a very smooth transition between games regarding the story. When that cutscene ends and gameplay starts initially, the first thing one notices is that the art style and visuals are very clean like the first game. It very much represents what the first game was visually, so if one was trying to convince someone else that this was the first game, then it would be believable because while it doesn’t necessarily look exactly the same, it's very reminiscent of the original game, and doesn't feel totally different, similar to the music. 
   Considering reminiscence one could also point to the UI specifically, which makes known that there is a difference between games. If one compares it to the early game, Circles are now replaced with hexagons, and colors are swapped. If one compares late game, all that really changes is that they simplified the textures, changed the space Ipad hexagon from green to purple, and shifted the character placement. If one moves their attention from off the top of the screen, whenever you click on something the click UI has changed from a hollowed out circle or hexagon with choices at the top and bottom, to it just being a filled in circle with choices at the top and bottom.
   Before one has the ability to click on every single item in the game and be curious like george, the first dialogue that is present really summarizes the state at which the characters are in with the storyline that catches you up pretty fast if you haven't played the first game recently...or if you just didn't press recap for some reason. They also have fourth wall breaks in the beginning of the game, which shows that self-aware humor is going to be very present in upcoming dialogue.
   The beginning area really gives us a glimpse of what’s to come by showing slivers of the art, humor, characters, and philosophy, which prepares us for the long journey ahead of us....also these guys really don’t matter other than introduce the mechanic where you get options of dialogue, red for Xefros, blue for Joey.
   Just when Joey was about to open the door, the enemy fleet at the very end of the first game crashes down, exploding the building...forcing the title card to appear. After the cut scene, we end up on a beach because apparently the dear cat just took us there thanks to exposition...at least there's some joking banter that’s actually quite humorous, mostly because one of the characters is trying to joke and the other one just doesn't understand the joke which makes it funny. This is a very common trope in this journey, because both characters make jokes except each of one responds in different ways, so the dynamic is Joey makes a lot of jokes and Xefros just can't take a joke because he is bluntly literal, and Joey isn’t. 
   When the gameplay starts at the beach, you start to notice that the walking animation during gameplay is extremely stuttery and the character looks like it has a white outline that’s horribly png'd...this is not ok. The first game did not have the outline problem, and the first game barely had this much stuttering. Every single time you move in this game it just looks bad...it’s not smooth, and at least not as smooth as the original game.
   The duo then ventures into the cave, aka, literally someone else’s home, and end up admiring an abstract form of a very schizophrenic art piece which spirals into a deep philosophical conversation about choice simply by drawing their own conclusions from personal experiences by interpreting art for literally 5 minutes straight. Besides that, the topic of not only taxidermy comes up: “it’s when you kill an animal...dominance over nature” (play clip), but finding some alien mushrooms in the cave digs up some deep rooted past trauma for Joey: “when I was little...stopped trusting anything he said” (play clip). These two situations are literally the only thing notable about this cave, simply because, that costume, that you were suppose to be looking for initially so that way Joey can blend in to this alien society...is not even in the cave....so turns out, the thing that you needed to progress the story, was in the garbage pile, you know...the thing you passed initially? Meaning the entire point of the cave is literally only for giving the characters a vehicle to share about their background, which is a great way to go about character development, rewarding the player for exploring...but it still feels like a total facepalm moment once you realize that it wasn’t even in the cave in the first place.
   Traversing through the hole in the cave leads you to a little village, where there are very cute cottages. Past that is the forest where Xefros and Joey venture into…it just gives you the option to just die if one’s curiosity gets the best of the cat, which was surprising and unexpected. This means that one has to find a way through the forest without killing cats, so Xefros and Joey head to the cottage, hoping to find something useful. This is where it’s naturally revealed that Xefros has psychic powers, and unlocks the door with it.
   In the cottage, a giant bug is just vibing in a cage. Xefros hands Joey the dance book, Joey finds some fake horns, which led to some unexpected humor that wasn’t previously expected to be in this game: (plays clip). Once Joey is ready to use the bee dance she learned from the book, the other unexpected thing occurred...a rhythm game...not kidding. Surprisingly fun, although it does take a round to really learn how to best maneuver the controls and timing, by round two, one feels like a professional osu player. Once the dance is done, the bug sprays it not says it, and coats Joey and Xefros in anxiety-reliving liquid that helps them get through the forrest.
   While being jealous of Joey and Xefros’ natural anxiety reliever, they make it to the train station. While exploring, the intercom guy in the station speaks some language that catches one off-guard, almost as if he’s muffled behind a dumpster in a back alley: (plays clip). Joey then goes up to the ticket counter to purchase two tickets, only to be immediately rejected due to blood color...so apparently, if you have the wrong blood color, the machine won't give you a ticket, leading us to the introduction of politics YAYYYYY
   In this specific society, there is a political/racial hierarchy separated by colors of blood. There are 12 colors in total: Fuchsia, Violet, Purple, Indigo, Cobalt, Teal, Olive, Lime, Yellow, Bronze, Burgundy, and Candy Red. Basically all you’ll really need to know currently is that any shade of purple or blue are higher in ranks.  
   Back in the train station, Joey and Xefros find another way to get some tickets, which leads them to talking to every single wacky character in the station. These vast range of characters each have their own dialogue quirks specific to them, so no matter who you talk to, you're always going to get a different experience, which makes each npc stand out...unless you’re one of two npcs...Zebruh...and Marvus. Overall, I enjoyed playing through Hiveswap Act 2: the art style was pleasing, the soundtrack was great and had several gems, the writing was on point and the story, while admittedly a bit on the boring side, was still something I enjoyed following. There are a LOT of different item and character interactions, a good amount of which brought a smile to my face as I was exploring the hellhole full of violence, death and segregation that is Alternia.

But the game has its flaws. It is too buggy for a game we've waited three years for, and I already had the same qualm for the previous game in the series. For example, I've had a handful of objects making me walk around the area for a good five seconds for no apparent reason upon inspecting them (the only one I can remember right now is the barnacle in the cave). In addition, it felt like the overall quality of the game's animated sequences had decreased quite a bit compared to Act 1's, which was especially noticeable during certain cutscenes.

What I found most annoying about this game though is how much backtracking the game makes you do towards the latter half of the story: while the things you did in-between the endless area switching you had to do were fine (pretty entertaining at times, too), the endless walking, door-opening, walking, door-opening, walking, escalator-using cycle made the story feel like it dragged on and on. That is a real shame, because I think I would have enjoyed this part of the story a lot more if it were not for the absurd amount of backtracking.

However, Act 2's saving grace is definitely the characters and their interactions with Joey and Xefros. Characters like Marvus, Tyzias and Elwurd made me feel like this whole ordeal was worth it - I have no doubt I wouldn't have bothered to finish the game if it didn't have such fun and interesting characters. I'd say this all culminated during the [strike]Phoenix Wright[/strike] legislaceration segment, which I thought was great fun and helped the characters shine. There are a few bad eggs here and there (Zebruh), but all in all, I really enjoyed getting to spend more time with the characters I got to meet in the Friendsim series.

Was this game worth the three years of waiting? No! The game felt way too short and buggy for it to be the case; if it had come out in Spring 2018, its initial release date, I wouldn't feel nearly as conflicted about it as I do now. Do I think this is still a good game? Well it sure has its flaws, but its upsides outweigh them just enough for me to be able to say Act 2 is at least a nice experience, at least in my opinion. I will absolutely lose my shit if Act 3 takes another 5 years to get released, though.

This is a good game with a lot of heart and soul. It's not a great game, but I definitely got my money's worth. I'd recommend it for anyone who wants more Homestuck in their life, but it's also good for anyone who wants an engaging game to blow though in a night.

The writing's good, but it's not quite "Homestuck". That may be due to the format though (and obviously that it's not pure Hussie). You're not getting chatlog walls of text; you're getting long conversations to click through. The story is also pretty focused around *CLASS DISPARITY* so it might come off as a little preachy, but it's not obnoxious and it's done competently. The characters are written wonderfully to give you a creeping, though not exactly subtle, realization that they're horrible...and WHY they're horrible. The two leads are likable the whole way through though. There were a few moments that made me *feel*, which means the writing did its job getting me invested. No hard laughs like the pigeons in Act 1 though.

Graphics and music are great and you can tell they thought through how they should be used to present the story. Easy to miss things like facial expressions and leitmotifs were accounted for.

The game has some problems, mostly that it can be obtuse at times. I managed to get through in one sitting without getting too frustrated or trying to look anything up though, so it's not too bad. There are some minor graphical issues, mainly with the way things pop in when a cutscene happens, but that's not really anything to care about. I'd like some more quality of life features for the conversations, but it's not a big deal. No crashes or game breaking bugs that I ran into (I'm on an older Mac laptop).

I'm surprised by the depth. There are a couple places where I know different choices could be made that would have an actual impact on things. There's at least one character that doesn't appear later because I sent him to his unwitting death, there's another I sentenced to death that could have been swapped for a guiltier party, and who knows how many other possibilities are out there. I don't think anything would change how it ends, but the journey is more important than the destination.

Overall, much improved from Act 1! Excited to see what's next!

Super game! The writing from the Homestuck folk is always so full of character, cheek, and intelligence (many of the devs here are writers first, gam devs second); the art is basically always gorgeous and rich; and there are a few moments that I think will stick with me for a long time.

Actually, let me mention one (maybe my favourite). Spoilers incoming!

So there's a long trial scene that serves as the centrepiece, I suppose, of the game. It's pretty hard to "win" it, and this is partly imo a fault of the devs' ability to see things through a new player's eyes - but also this isn't really a serious weakness, because here, as elsewhere, the fail-states are also really good. One in particular is I think one of my favourite moments from *any* game. Right, so in this trial, if you follow the evidence in one direction, you get plausible guilt for someone who you honestly think might've done the crime in question (Lynera). In fact she didn't do it, though! You're told this by your guide (Tyzias) after the fact. Your character, Joey, is understandably mad as hell at Tyzias for not stepping in before the verdict came in that unjustly damned Lynera. Tyzias's whole schtick is that she's fighting for reform of the legal system in Alternia (which is grossly, cartoonishly unjust) - but she's okay with injustice getting done anyway!?

Tyzias explains herself to you: She shares your ideals of people not getting done in for crimes they didn't do, but it's not possible to reform the extant legal system that radically that quickly. Justice is still entertainment and still has to maintain social order. Reforming it has to be done gradually or not at all.

This is obviously an allegory for the sort of incrementalist political strategy we get in real life too; and here, too, it is tempting, and often seems like the only possible outcome. But here, too, it has the immediate consequence of people having their lives ruined for no good reason. Hiveswap enacts this tension really marvellously. 

And this is the outcome if you *fail* the game! Now that's a mark of seriously good game-making.

I don't want to sound as if I have no problems with the game. It needs polish at various points; how to do a thing is often unintuitive (though is the ameliorated somewhat by the help button that always has what you need); and there's a general sense of pedestrianness in the game that I can't articulate, but which I think is to do with how little the overall quest, or the frame of the game, changes over its course. You're still basically the same person at the end as you were at the beginning, and this seems a little complacent, as if you (or your character, or "us") doesn't need to develop as a person, or as if she/we have nothing left to learn. But against this, it should be remembered here that this is only Act 2 of a much larger story. Maybe I'm being unfair to expect so much of this.

So anyway - great game: great writing, lovely art, lots of jokes and some great philosophy... check it out!

Shockingly sad at some parts :( but it made me invested! Like I got up around my room and did laps through the house like "ohhh damn I gotta do this Im so scared what will happen dear god" kind of invested! 

Tho a biggest flaw is not being able to go back and read text that I skip on accident or to catch up my memory. very easy to get confused in that case. Once you skip a line of text you might not be able to replay the interaction to see what they said :(

Cons:
Unlike Act 1, Hiveswap Act 2 has a weird relationship with the inventory system. Over half the time, when you obtain an item that you need to show to someone else, it doesn't go into your inventory. It doesn't go anywhere at all, you simply have to remember that your character is holding onto it, and will then offload it when you talk to the relevant person. I ask, if they were going to do that, then why have an inventory system at all? It's highly baffling.

A significant portion of Hiveswap Act 2 is a love letter to Ace Attorney, giving you similar gameplay. I love the fact that the devs did this. They nailed the music and the graphics very well! But the gameplay itself falls very short, sadly. I've played almost all the Ace Attorney games, I'm very familiar with them. And yet, almost every step of the way, I was utterly baffled about which evidence to present to which testimony while I was playing Hiveswap. It doesn't make sense, so I got it wrong over and over. The game's requirement of which evidence to present where... just doesn't follow any logic I can decipher. Given how much I like the idea of a love letter to Ace Attorney in Hiveswap form, it was disappointing to see how poorly the logic-writing fell flat.

Pros:
Luckily, that bad logic-writing did not carry over to any other portion of the game. Everything else you need to do to progress does make sense.

After three long years since Act 1 (and several long years during which Act 1 was in development), Hiveswap: Act 2 represents the second of four planned games (which will only be a half of the larger Hiveswap/Hauntswitch story). If this is news to you, this probably isn't a game with much to offer for you. For those who are still interested in Homestuck, this is worth picking up. 

Compliments: 
The backgrounds in this game are very pretty, the music's good, the dialogue (which makes up the majority of the game) is well-written and enjoyable, and it was a joy to get to know the characters from Friendsim I'm a different way. It takes about eight hours to play, which is about twice as long as Act 1. Because of a variety of paths you can take to solve various puzzles, the game offers some replay value, though it's not a game you're likely to play again and again. 

Critiques: 
The long narration when investigating every little thing has mostly given way to dialogue (which may be a fair trade). The section of the game during which you meet the midbloods has a very long parody of another game style, which I enjoyed but those who aren't fans of the genre may not. There are some continuity errors that are annoying but not deal breakers - things dropped from Act 1, some inconsistencies within some dialogue, that sort of thing. Two of the Friendsim trolls do not appear in the game. The introductory areas feel like they should have been cut content - you walk through three areas before anything happens. None of that really impacted my enjoyment of the game, but my biggest problem is that it has no fast forward button for what's essentially a gussied up visual novel. It makes replaying tedious. 

Act 1 Considerations: 
The developers say you don't need to play Act 1 to play Act 2, and that's true - there's not that much plot you'll miss out on if you miss it. But, in order to get the best outcome on a certain puzzle, you do need to import save data from Act 1. Download some if you haven't played it. 

Overall, I would recommend this game to anyone who's not tired of exploring Alternia. I enjoyed the characters and lore a lot. For those who aren't already steeped in Homestuck and Friendsim, however, this would probably offer less to enjoy.

Hmm, a bit of a divide I'm seeing at the moment regarding Act 2. Allow me to give my 2 cents.

It's not quite what I expected for the follow-up to Act 1, taking place mostly in one location (the train), and I feel that it suffers slightly for it. BUT I still had a good time and appreciate what Act 2 offered. Allow me to go into further detail, addressing some criticisms.

The most odd and immediate criticism I see is regarding the Bee-focused mini-game that happens early-on. 

[b][u]Note: It seemed at first as if said mini-game was removed due to backlash, but in actuality it was made optional. I never thought it was that difficult in the first place and I go more into my more fresh opinions on what it's like to play through it in a moment, but here is my breakdown of the complaints of it nonetheless.[/u][/b]

People who are less-inclined to rhythm games or otherwise have some manner of chronic pain or disability may find it difficult, especially working from a keyboard. While my heart goes out to those who cannot get past this spot due to physical conditions, I personally don't believe myself to be that skilled in that type of game mechanic and I still got the hang of it after 3-5 tries. So that's the advice I can offer to those who simply didn't pass it due to lack of skill. For people in either scenario, though, I believe the community has shared save files now for just-beyond the Bee mini-game so with that helping hand they can proceed on their own.

The next largest bout of criticism would be the Ace Attorney-parody section that takes place in the Teal/Jade train car. Some of the most invalid criticism, admittedly, would be about the change in art style. Which baffles me. It's an Ace Attorney parody, so of course the art style would be a part of it. Plus, the more detailed "Hero Mode" kind of sprites have been a thing in Homestuck for a while, especially FriendSim and Pesterquest. That complaint came across to me as idiotic.

However, there is some way I feel about the Ace Attorney segment too. While I appreciate the parody and set-up, it did take a little longer in the playthrough than I'd like. Not to mention the juggling of save files and inventory management needed to get the Best Possible Ending for the trial. It was during this segment I was REALLY wanting the ability to save anywhere, or at least fast forward through the text as, as someone who explored all avenues possible to gain all achievements for this game, this was one of the most tedious sections to need to repeat. Some people complain about the difficulty or randomness of the section as well, that the answers could have made more blatantly logical sense. However, I never saw this as an obstacle, considering the generous amount of tips Tyzias is able to provide.

There are more flaws to the structure I could point out too. The bulk of the quests in the Highblood and Clown Cars felt like busy work and padding the most, being predictable quests that follow the Rule of 3. Ace Attorney section aside, the minor puzzles in the Lowblood Cars felt like they were pulled off better, though I do appreciate the ingenuity needed for the Clowns.

Some people think this game isn't long enough too, which I disagree with. Looking at my recorded playtimes between Acts 1 and 2 (and I went for 100% achievement completion for both), Act 2 indeed took me roughly 2-3x the length of Act 1, just as they promised. I would have more to complain about the execution than the length itself.

There is evidence of cut content regarding the character of Zebede and Charun, who are characters that were introduced in FriendSim but didn't make an appearance in this game. However, while it would lengthen the game, I can't expect it would have done much for flow, as evidence suggests their role would be more in mini-games concerning fishing and sculpting respectively. More mini-games before we even get on the train, in other words. I can only see that bloating the end product, so I can see why it would be cut. We'll probably get to meet them later.

But now, all those concerns addressed, I feel like I've still been too negative. We've been waiting for this for so long and, while not perfect, I really enjoyed this Act too. I eagerly await Act 3. And Joey's Hoodie Disguise, complete with Dammek's sign and troll horns, are on sale on For Fans By Fans and honestly that's the best piece of merch idea they've had in a while. Oh, and the soundtrack is always killer.

TLDR: The game is fine, but not outstanding. It's perfectly mediocre. Get it if you've already played the first one, skip it if you don't know what Homestuck is.

This will not be a spoiler-free review.

========= The Good =========
- Music is lovely, Toby Fox and James Roach always know how to deliver. I love the evolution of the train theme and the variations that play throughout. The serene music in the beginning is great, with Charun's cave entrance (Above Sea Level) and Zebede's farm (Raw Honey).
- Characters are written very well and consistent to what I expect based off of Hiveswap Friendsim. I loved the moments that surprised me the most, such as when a character who I thought I knew does something I didn't know they would do. It was always a pleasant surprise. For example, Wanshi is adorable, but when she sells out and frames Lynera it's all the more surprising and its impact resounds. Similarly, it's really interesting to see Bronya's more stern side when she's upset with her group. Those are just some examples, and there are plenty more in the game.
- I like the dancing bee minigame, it's actually pretty good. Why they removed it is beyond me. Accessibility issues, my ass- this is easily solvable by making it optional. I wish the game could've had more minigames, it would've made the game feel more engaging.
- The "typical" outcome of the trial. Oh man, I think this is like the most emotionally impactful the game has been for me. Seeing a character removed from the game like that? Amazing. It really makes me feel like my actions had consequences and gives the game lots of replay value making me want to explore different paths to see how I can get an ending that satisfies me.
- The background art is wonderful, and the sprite animations are just so full of life!
- Let's get to the big nitty-gritty of it all. The purpose of this game is to be an illustrated vertical slice of Alternia's social dynamics and the problems that come with it. To newcomers, it introduces the alien culture of Alternia with a colorful cast of some of Alternia's best and worst. To long-time fans, it delves deeper into some of the lore of the world. I think the game does a good enough job to do both. With that, it also provides character growth for our two main protagonists: Joey and Xefros. Joey learns the harsh truth of what Alternia is really like, starting off with cute and fun minigames and ending with a brutal crushing of her innocence. Xefros learns to be more independent and come to his own conclusions of what he wants to see come from the upcoming Rebellion that he's been part of the whole time. I think that the game does a fair job doing just that, but let's put a pin on that.

========= Areas of Improvement =========
- Charun and Zebede's exclusion usually wouldn't be the first thing, but the fact that we visit their respective homes and they're conspicuously absent leaves a bad taste in my mouth. Knowing that Charun potentially had a minigame associated with his section as well is really hearbreaking since I wanted more minigames.
- While I commended the animations earlier for being full of life, I do have to point out that animation transitions are not smooth. Some animations like when characters switch from one talking animation to another just feel too jarring without proper transitions. Similarly, the cutscenes feel lackluster as well. Some animations are so fast that I don't get time to digest what I just saw!
- The trial is not bad, but it does take a long time and monopolizes the experience. Had it been shorter or easier to solve, it would've been a much better experience in line with everything else. Either make all the puzzles as memorable and long lasting as the trial or make the trial easier. It was laughable how easy the gold/olive train car was compared to the jade/teal train car- Azdaja's strife theme is such a delight but players never get the full experience of the song if the sequence lasts but a few seconds! The fact that the trial overshadows the rest of the puzzles is not a good thing.
- Returning to the topic of "choices matter," I wish that the game gave me the opportunity to make more choices? This is perhaps my biggest area of improvement for the game. I'm well aware of all the results of the trial, but I think making it so that the trial had more potential characters to get rid of would be a great addition to the story. Similarly, I wish that all puzzles had like, multiple ways of solving them but no one set way. For example, the train ticket dilemma was very good because there were multiple ways to approach the problem, but I feel like the burgundy/bronze cart, the gold/olive cart, and the cerulean/indigo cart had such straightforward answers that rather than making choices I felt like I was just on a single set path. I wish that there were multiple ways to answer the same problem so that players can be rewarded when they solve the problem with a better answer.
- The game doesn't do enough to make me care about some of these characters. I've played Friendsim, so I know and love these characters already but if I didn't play Friendsim, I couldn't care less about who these people are or why I'm invested in them. Do you know who I ended up caring about the most? Folykl. She was important in three separate interactions (train station, gold/olive puzzle, and cerulean/indigo puzzle) and she made the biggest impact as a Trollcall character. The reason Lynera's conviction was so gripping was because I already loved her from the Friendsim, but if I didn't play it, I wouldn't care that she got the short end of the stick and got killed off, which wouldn't drive me to find a solution where none of the characters get killed off. It's Act 2 and I barely even care about Joey, and she's the main character! Homestuck's strength has always been the fact that it was character-driven and it's the interactions that make these characters so loveable. The jades and the teals are memorable because they took the spotlight. Please do the same for the other trolls, it was heartbreaking to see fan favorites like Boldir and Remele and Mallek and have like only a handful of lines come from them. What was even the point of including Diemen and Vikare in the car if they werent going to do anything? What was the purpose of some of these characters? Why were they part of the build up of the game if they were going to either get axed from the final product or not have any speaking role beyond being part of the background?

========= Final Thoughts =========
I love Homestuck and I want to see it thrive. I'm well aware of the game's tumultuous past, but I feel that this game just delivered only enough to warrant a passing grade. I do not want to recommend this game because I think that the fans deserve better, but I reluctantly will. I can't say that the game didn't make me smile or care a little bit, but if I want more from the game, I need to continue to support it and make sure it gets the best life.

I consider this game to be an improvement over Hiveswap Act 1, but ultimately it should still appeal to the same people (and most of those people will want to play act 1 first).

As before, it's effectively a visual novel disguised as a point and click adventure. However, despite most of it being literally on-rails this one has more legitimate puzzles and requires you to think a bit. The focus is almost entirely on social interactions with the trolls you meet, rather than "use item X on background object Y", which is a great change from traditional point-and-click fare and really plays to the author's strengths.

And yes, Andrew Hussie is in peak form here. The characters you meet are all fun and quite varied, the scenarios they place you in are creative, and several puzzles have more than one solution you can find. The story is focused on the parts of Homestuck's lore that everyone already found most interesting. The worldbuilding holds up with or without knowledge of the prior work. The comedy and character development is on point. There's plenty of silly secret remarks you can get from using every item on every person or talking to people at different points in the story, but since you're actually TALKING to people it doesn't hurt the pacing much this time. And the change in format renders it 100% immune to the pacing problems that Homestuck itself suffered from.

That being said, the brief portion at the start of the game where there AREN'T a lot of characters around suffers from the same slow pacing as Act 1. Maybe even worse since not much is happening.

Don't worry about difficulty. Most puzzles can eventually be solved by just talking to everyone about everything, and the one section with deeper puzzles (the trial) has a hint button that starts vague but will hand you the answer if you hit it enough times. There's no other skill-based minigames (one got removed and if it gets readded it'll probably be skippable) so anyone should be able to beat this game.

The game is longer than Act 1. Took me about 13 hours to complete (with moderate reloading to explore other options), compared to 8 on the first game. For replay value, there's a lot of hidden achievements based on the multiple ways of solving certain puzzles, on preserving certain items for the whole run, etc. In fact you'd need several full playthroughs to get all acheivements since some are mutually exclusive. But since you can't fast forward dialog I have a hard time imagining myself doing more than just a second playthrough (not counting reloads just before a part I want to retry).

Some people on the forums complained about bugs and softlocks, but I didn't see a single one in my play experience.

Overall, anyone who liked Homestuck, or even liked parts of Homestuck, will probably love this game. And Act 2 is better than Act 1. But I'd still suggest playing Act 1 before Act 2.

Hiveswap Act 2 is an amazing continuation of Hiveswap, featuring much more content and interesting material compared to Act 1. The majority of this game involves talking with the many Trolls of Alternia, learning their culture, making friends, and completing tasks to progress the story. A major improvement over the first game is the branching options for completing tasks, resulting in different outcomes and scenarios that will continue into the next Act. Your inventory from the previous game’s save can also impact this. The cast of trolls to interact with is greatly varied and personably, with lots of fun dialogue and different personalities. For fans of Homestuck, this is a great source for additional lore, while being an approachable introduction to Alternian society to newcomers to the series. The visual and animation quality seems slightly worse compared to Act 1, but still very charming and presentable. The music is well composed and very catchy, although lacking in variety due to an overarching leitmotif for most of the game. This is one of the few places the first Act outshines the game. Backtracking becomes annoying for multiple playthroughs and the lack of keyboard controls can lead to sore hands, but these are the only major problems with the game. Tailing points based on several attributes (Story: 10/10, Gameplay: 8/10, Controls: 7/10, Content: 7/10, Presentation: 9/10, Music: 9/10, Performance: 8/10, 58/70 total), this game scores an 83/100. For anyone who played Act 1 or enjoys Homestuck, this is a must play.

TL;DR fans who are still invested in the homestuck IP will find this game engaging, especially if they played the friendsim. however, i found the second half of the game tedious as well as the puzzles unintuitive and irritating. some material feels like it was stretched out to make it a longer game than act 1, but there is a lot of exposition to find around every corner. if youre invested in alternia as a concept and enjoy talking to random trolls, youll find something to appreciate.

longer notes ahead, with spoilers....

given its fraught development history, act 2 is substantially meatier than act 1 and feels very clean, sleek, and thought out with a mostly friendly UI design. there is perhaps a little too much flavor text, which led me to wasting a lot of time in my first playthrough just clicking random combinations.

the first half of the game is adorable, visually engaging, but a little unbalanced. the real challenge comes with a rhythm game that... doesnt seem to follow the rhythm much, and it took me a few tries to accomplish it. i was also disappointed when others pointed out that a good chunk of content appears to have been cut, perhaps to push the game out faster? which, at this point, seems arbitrary given how long it was delayed! :P though there wasnt much to do, i really enjoyed the time spent outside of the train platform. i loved studying the gorgeous backgrounds and finding little expository details.

the format of fighting your way up through the train to get a sampling of what life is like for each caste was a smart one, and i appreciated as someone who never played friendsim that our interactions with the trolls were like readers digest versions of their routes (though, admittedly i was far more interested in the trolls i couldnt click on). xefros' explanations of alternia cater to people who are unfamiliar with the homestuck IP, which wasnt a bad thing and didnt feel boring to me as someone who already knew the trolls whole deal. however, reaching the jade/teal train is when my feelings on the game really started to falter. spoilers ahead.

interactions between the jades and teals felt hamfisted at times in an attempt to make the game more edgy/nsfw, with innuendos serving only to confuse the naive and oblivious joey, which had already been established by her interactions with an older drug dealer. the trial took me hours without a guide and overwhelmed me with tedium. it largely felt like filler material to make the game longer than act 1, and i felt irritated and disinterested with the trial as a whole. framing lynera left me feeling dissatisfied and confused, and even after going back with the right materials and confronting wanshi, i knew i had made the right choice but still felt the same dissatisfaction. if youre a fan of ace attorney, maybe youll get more out of the experience than i did.

moving on from teal and going up to blue, my irritation with the puzzle mechanics and hint function escalated. after encountering some minor bugs like joey getting stuck in the ceiling of the elevator, i found myself getting repeatedly confused with the hint function basically useless. nihkees quest took me a frustratingly long time involving tedious back-and-forth up and down the train before i finally stumbled accidentally into the solution of simply... agreeing to be catfished by ardata again? it figures that the truly mystifying part of this game for me was figuring out how to impress a lesbian.

additionally, the hint function can be surprisingly mean-spirited considering the unintuitive puzzle mechanics as well as... the sheer amount of time and radio silence it took for this game to come out! you cannot both mock your players stupidity and ask for their money at the same time, but unfortunately this seems to be a trend for this IP. at times, it feels as though the developers of this game are far more skilled with writing than they are with designing a player friendly game.

as you can expect, the purple car brought on a significant tone shift. the car itself was gorgeously designed, and i enjoyed looking at everything the way i did in the first part of the game. marvus' killing game was much more straightforward than i thought it would be, though the return of pacing back and forth down the train was incredibly monotonous i still figured out how to trick them without guidance. i was also engaged most by the design of the purples, so i was very sad to see baizli... well, you know. :o(

moving onto the control room, i got several game overs simply by taking too long to disable the drone. this part is incredibly frustrating and made me groan and fuss quite a lot. you WILL need a guide or to spam the hint button to figure out what to do, and the final step of throwing a pet treat and getting byers to peck at the drones brain meats was especially exasperating. imagine how angry i was to have finally gotten the train on the right route... only to have the train immediately derail. what was the point of all that labor, then? it felt pointless and futile, and while the cutscene was interesting it moved too quickly and left a bad taste in my mouth.

as someone who is pretty uninterested in alternia, this game managed to engage me with beautiful visuals and intriguing character design. however, parts of the game felt hamfisted, as if after all this time the developers still arent quite sure how to design a point-and-click adventure game. solutions are usually far from obvious, and you can expect a lot of frustration if you arent getting your hand held by a walkthrough. luckily, the sheer amount of things to look at are usually a good distraction from totally ragequitting - when wandering confused through the blue car i found myself just staring at the wonderfully rendered decorations. in future acts - if they get that far ;o) - the team should consider cutting out fluff and flavor text, as well as improving a passive aggressive and patronizing hint function.

MUSIC

If you're a fan of leitmotifs, you'll love this game. With a soundtrack created by the talented James Roach and Toby Fox, creator of Undertale, you know you're in for tunes that will get stuck in your head

GAMEPLAY

This game is a 2020 reimagining of classic Point and Click adventure games. You'll feel nostalgic while also getting a fresh new experience

STORY

The character interactions make up the bulk of this game, and it's certainly worth it. The characters are fun, quirky, and sassy. Everyone you talk to is a pleasure to get to know, and the game is even better when the characters talk to each other, especially in the Jade/Teal car.

Where to begin? Man, I could write a whole ass essay about this game, but I'll spare you all and just list some pros and cons! Spoilers below!

Cons:
- God just... The entire ace attorney trial. That was a nightmare. It was so drawn out and kind of pointless? especially since the game doesn't tell you, that you need to keep your items to trade with tagora for the right information. Another point is, that information that is necessary to proceed is held from you and only when the plot calls for it, do characters actually give you the information. Such as one ponit where you're literally just supposed to present wrong evidence (because you don't have any proof) until one of the characters gives you the info you need to continue.
- A general problem my friend and I found while playing, is that at times, you find yourself trying everything on everything, because the game doesn't communictae how you should proceed. We had to look up a walkthrough to get past some of it. Clicking everything randomly kind of takes away from the experience.
- Maybe highlighting the items you can interact with and every character you can talk to would be a good idea? Because it is extremely easy to miss areas, since some of the things you can check aren't that obvious.
- Didn't let us hold Elwurd's hand (my friend was very upset about this)

Now onto the positives!
Pros:

I will say that for the amount of time I waited for this game, it was honestly pretty lackluster. Taking nearly 3 years from the release of Act 1, and putting fans through thoughts that we weren't even going to get another part of the game, and that it was simply going to end on Act 1. The feeling of excitement that everyone felt as soon as we had a release date, and furthering that feeling once the game actually dropped was something that a lot of us expected to never feel. This being said, the final product after everything the developers put fans through, was honestly pretty mediocre from where the first part of the game stands. 

I remember when Act 1 first came out and spending my entire night beating it and being absolutely amazed at the art, characters, and story line that was coming out based on my favorite comic. So many times during that first game was I absolutely blown away at where the story line was taking me and the breathtaking art that only furthered the nostalgia. [h1] HIVESWAP: Act 2 [/h1]

Around two years ago, Hiveswap Act 2 released. Fans of this series had to wait a while for this game to be released. As someone who remembers seeing the trailer for this game before it came out, I was excited to meet a variety of Trolls, each with a unique personality. However, at the time, I didn't have access to the DLC packs of Hiveswap Friendism Simulator. Even today, I have not played Friendism Simulator quite yet so keep this in mind when I explain my thoughts about this game and the mixed bag of an experience it is.

[h1] Characters [/h1]

If there is one thing that helps Act 2 be enjoyable, it is the characters. We are introduced to a bunch of new Trolls, ranging from across the Hemospectrum (a way to describe the twelve blood colours). From rustbloods like Marsti to high ranking purplebloods, like Marvus. All of the Trolls feel unique to each other and fit in with some of the aspects associated with some of the Troll blood colours (Tealbloods are typically law abiding and Jadebloods are typically nuns and female). The differences between the Troll Blood Castes helps players understand some of the views towards certain Blood Castes. If there is one thing about the characters that is slightly annoying, it is that you only really interact heavily with some of them, with some Blood Castes (like Olivebloods, Indigobloods and Bronzebloods) don't get much attention. This is mainly due to the fact that a substantial portion of the game takes place in the cart of Jadebloods and Tealbloods. Still, the game does help those not familiar with Homestuck understand Trolls and their society.

[h1] Gameplay [/h1]

The gameplay of Act 2 is quite similar to Act 1. However, there is a lot more branching paths, leading to more achievements taking longer to complete. One aspect of gameplay that is unique to Act 2 is a trial, in a very similar format to the Ace Attorney franchise. Apart from that however, there is a lot of backtracking when on the train, which can be annoying when it takes a while to travel to places. 

[h1] Story [/h1]

Act 2 immediately takes place after Act 1, where Joey and Xefros escape from the Empress' forces. After helping disguise Joey as a Troll, the two of them get some tickets (mainly through the help of some of the Trolls) and catch the train. Joey, however, receives an alarming message from a Troll named Fiamet. She has only 11 days to travel back through the portal she arrived in before Alternia (the Troll planet) and Earth are destroyed. Joey and Xefros have to find a way to get to Jeevik Week in order to get help from Cridea Jeevik, the one hosting the event. If they want to get there quickly, they are going to need to get to the front of the train to speed things up. Overall, I'd say the story for Act 2 is quite straightforward. But, things are still left unexplained. Hopefully, these things are explained in the next Act or else there is going to be a lot of questions needing answers.

[h1] Conclusion [/h1]

Hiveswap Act 2 improves upon Act 1 but still has it's issues. Thankfully, players can legitimately obtain all of the achievements. But note that many of them are rewarded for going down alternate paths. Players would need to do a minimum of two playthroughs. One of them is where the player obtains all of the Game overs. To do this, when you receive a game over, click on the screen and wait for it to load with where you were before the game over. Do not load up a save previously before the game over as that will not count. The other playthrough is achieved through not dying at all. It is also important to note that you will need a save from Act 1 with the batteries still in the inventory. These are essential to get some of the achievements. Overall, if you liked the first game and want to know more about the Trolls, you will like this game. For new players, however, I'd heavily recommend playing Act 1 first.

Rating - 7/10 (The game improves on Act 1 but die hard fans will be left with a brutal cliffhanger. It is also important to note that the future of Hiveswap and the potential game Hauntswitch are left ambiguous due to What Pumpkin not exactly being the greatest of companies and any details about Hiveswap development are not told until a few weeks before a release)
