This is a really tough one to review. Overall, I say "Recommend," because it's an audacious and quality work, and the makers deserve money for it. Do I think most people would enjoy this game, as a game? No.

It's not like HIVESWAP: Act 1, which was a straightforward point-n-click adventure game. That was standard--observe the environment, find the items, find the obstacles, use the items on the obstacles, progress. The setting and writing were quirky and neat, the puzzles fair.

Act 2 has a little of that, but only a very little. In Act 1, near the end, the game shifts into a new kind of game, that is almost straight-up visual novel told through dialogue, until the end. Act 2 carries this on. It is almost entirely dialogue-driven, with almost no point-n-click puzzling. The solutions are nearly all 1) Talk to character, 2) Talk to other character, 3) talk to original character.

Part of this is really impressive. While you're progressing, at every turn, every character--and there are a great many characters, each with a unique, consistent voice--has new things to say. For an adventure game, that is remarkable. Every one of them weighs in, helpfully or not, on every part of every puzzle. Huge amounts of dialogue.

Unfortunately, this ends up making the game-play a series of "talk to every character about everything," over and over again. This gets brainless and not fun.

A huge portion of the story is very similar to--to the point of near plagiarism--Snowpiercer. It's a shame that this is so shameless, because if it weren't for this piracy, it's a very-well-told cosmology of class distinction, class envy, class callousness, and class struggle. But it is far too close to Snowpiercer, complete with advancing-through-train-one-car-at-a-time, to give this game full credit.

Finally: The Phoenix Wright pastiche is *interminable.* It just goes on, and on, and on, and ON, AND ON, and the novelty wears out far, far before the sequence ends. The whole part is a joke, and an obvious one, but then it just refuses to let go, and this goes on for something like a half-hour of straight dialogue. This was a horrible choice.

I've been a Homestuck fan since 2012, I joined shortly before the Kickstarter for Hiveswap came out. I wasn't able to contribute at the time because I was quite young, but I've kept my excitement and eagerness to see this series come to fruition since, even despite so many people angrily DEMANDING for the next installment when things kept being delayed more and more.

Sure, there have been hiccups along the way, and the Fandom has grown more and more divisive. On top of that, the extended wait, and the existence of the Friendsim series, have only amped up the hype through the ages. As I said, I've stayed optimistic, more than a lot of other fans, and more than even some friends of mine, but even then, that building hype, the delays, I kept my expectations tempered. Still as the date approached I got more and more excited, and now that I have finally been able to play through and finish it?

The wait was well damn worth it. I am not going to say this game is flawless. I am not going to say this is an immense masterpiece. But I do love it to bits and has surpassed my expectations for this series somehow. The Maturity Rating actually helps this game shine even more, when it refuses to back down from the brutality of Alternia, and the jokes they pull off, it literally had me laughing out loud and shouting and doing spit-takes at several points through the whole story. The characters are charming, there's SO much dialogue, there's so many different options of things to go through, and despite having put 11 hours into this game at the time of writing this, I still feel like I am missing several major secrets along the way. I haven't even clicked everything with every item in my inventory yet!

The cutscenes, the backgrounds, the character animations. Every piece of dialogue. The little puzzles and fetch quests, and several scenes I will not spoil, but that if you have played the game, know EXACTLY what I am thinking about despite not even alluding to the nature of them- Yeah it was just fun.

I had SOME minor trouble with a few of the objects, but 'click the specific item' is kind of a thing with Point and Clicks, but also I'm dumb? And I was streaming this so I wasn't at my 100%, and there IS a Hint System, so I can't even really complain about that.

Ultimate though, seriously. If you're a Homestuck Fan, or a Point and Click fan, or even if it just seems visually charming? I wholeheartedly recommend this game. I have waited for this Act to come out for quite a while, and I will GLADLY wait however much longer they may need to get the rest of the series out.

What Pumpkin is just really, REALLY bad at marketing; I didn't even know Act 2 had come out until months after it released. The artwork is top-notch, the soundtrack is iconic, and the little hints to what may or may not be going on just beneath the surface are downright delicious. My main problem with this game is honestly the way it wasted my time. Act 2 boasts a far longer runtime than Act 1 (probably because people complained that Act 1 ended almost as quickly as it started) and the writing team decided to lengthen the runtime in this game by making the story grind to a screeching halt. The Trial was honestly the absolute worst part of this entire game. Up until the Trial, the game's story progresses quite smoothly and the pacing is good. The point-and-click style of gameplay fits the narrative and compliments the rest of the plot nicely up until this point. The Trial portion of this game decided to completely ruin the gameplay.
Vague spoilers from here on out! I won't be revealing any specific details of the story, just how the gameplay irritated me a lot.
The Trial thrives off the idea that it can be Ace Attorney. If you've every played an Ace Attorney game then youll know it absolutely fails on this aspect. The collection of evidence and testimonies in Hiveswap Act 2 is when the gameplay becomes the fatal flaw of the narrative. Running around to constantly talk to the same trolls over and over again is so tedious. It isn't engaging at all, and the point-and-click nature of hiveswap makes it infuriating to get anything done during this portion of the game. Imo the Trial was just included to pad the story because that is essentially all it does. It adds absolutely nothing to the plot and just exists to give the game a longer runtime. Even the game gave me a pitiful message of "wow that was pointless" Really fucking annoying to go through all that nonsense and receive absolutely nothing out of it. The moment the game stops being fun is the moment you should know you failed. After the Trial, the game continues to let the narrative drag the unwilling player (and also Joey) along for the ride. The whole time I was playing I honestly just wanted to put the game down because of the constant backtracking and the hint function making me feel like an idiot for not understanding the fucking convoluded bullshit this game was putting me through. The point-and-click nature of the game made doing anything at all become extremely frustrating. Going back and talking to irritating npcs was beyond frustrating and i felt like the game was wasting my time with pointless quests and really irritating parts of the narrative. the story was no longer actually interesting and started to feel extremely frustrating. Honestly by the end of the game i felt like i was Joey Claire because I just wanted to get the fuck off alternia and never look back.

Man this will probably get buried because who the hell is reading reviews for Hiveswap games other than absolutely maniacal diehard Homestucks who don't care if the game is any good or not. But I'll say it anyway:

Act 1 is a mediocre point and click adventure game carried by the charm of the characters and the themes of the original "comic".

Act 2 is a really shitty point and click adventure game to the point where the writing couldn't carry it no matter how good it was, but also the writing is not as good as Act 1's (although still way better than the gameplay).

Act 1's puzzles were typical adventure game fare, of apply the item in the situation for it. Act 2's puzzles are just, talk to all of the trolls. Then talk to all of the trolls again. There is nothing to interact with in Act 2 except for the characters and you don't even get good characterization out of that because there's like 30 different characters. The shitty game design absolutely climaxes in the "trial" sequence during which it's not enough to have the right pieces of evidence, or know which pieces apply to which testimonies, you have to read the game's mind on exactly when and in what order to present things, including some absolutely nonsensical tangents that you're required to launch to actually get through tot he end. No one got through this game without a walkthrough unless they methodically trial-and-errored their way through that shitshow because it makes ABSOLUTELY NO SENSE.

A dissapointing sequel to the hype Act 1 and the long wait built. Where the first game had too few (maybe none?) game-over scenarios, this one has too many.  Roughly 2/5ths through the game I would start getting game-overs left and right. I have no idea how someone is supposed to get the flawless playthrough achievement without using a guide, which in my opinion is the WORST way to experience an adventure game on your first run.
Furthermore, I spotted several times the sylladex system simply wasn't used. Inn the myriad fetchquests you need to do on the train-car, I spotted several times where an item wasn't put into Joey's/Xefros' sylladex, and was simply passed through via initiating dialogue. While this could be forgiven if it was consistent, the game starts using the sylladex again later.
The horrid icing on the crummy cake was the final strife and ending cutscene. I absolutely could NOT have beaten the drone flawlessly unless I abused the hint system constantly, which, again, is not an enjoyable experience. Unless you the player are an Alternian bio-engineer, even if you killed the drone without fail,you will probably get a game-over thinking it's safe to divert the tracks, only to get a game-over without ANY cutscene or dialogue telling you WHY you got it.
If you're a diehard Homestuck/Hiveswap fan, pick this up on sale and use a guide- otherwise, if you still want to see the story, wait for your favorite Let's Player or Walkthrough channel to post.

If you really enjoyed the first game, be aware that this one is a completely different experience. Instead of rooms full of a multitude of objects that can be interacted with lots of different ways with funny dialogue, Act 2 focuses much more on character dialogue, the rooms being otherwise mostly empty and with little opportunity to use your items. If you enjoyed the Hiveswap Friendsim, you might like this new dialogue-focused approach; otherwise you will probably find a lot of this game quite boring. Friendsim fans should also be aware that the Friendsim's story has zero effect on how the characters are portrayed in this game, so you shouldn't expect this to be anything like a true sequel to Friendsim either.

Beyond that, it's obvious this Act of the game is an unfinished product. It's quite evident that a lot of content has been cut from the first few rooms of the game, which are also the largest. Among this cut content are the characters Zebede and Charun, who were advertised as Act 2 characters years ago and were included in promotional art for the game even within a month of the game's release. No explanation has been given for why these characters in particular are simply absent from the finished product, but a rushed release is quite apparent.

Even beyond the content that was obviously originally in the game and then removed, a lot of Act 2's features are half finished, and features from Act 1 are totally missing. The Chittr or Prongle social media mechanic that has been advertised since before even the release of Act 1 is almost non existent, being used only for a single scene plus some minor gags early in the game - and need it be stated that we are now halfway through the originally planned length of Hiveswap. Despite Act 2 having a lot of puzzles that are much more difficult than Act 1, the sparkles that indicated useful items in the first Act are now gone. Instead you will be expected to use the hint feature, which for some reason only works for one of the two playable characters.

The game looks quite good, and aside from some inconsistent and at times hard to understand GUI, it functions mostly how a point and click adventure game should function. However those expecting the tight, witty writing from the original Homestuck and Act 1 should probably try looking elsewhere. And unfortunately, so should anyone expecting their money to be going toward an actual finished product worthy of the years it took to hit shelves.

So, I think this is my first ever thumbs down review for a video game. And I feel kinda bad about that, since I really *really* want to like this game. 

I'll start by being nice. The presentation is a step-up from Act 1, clearing up some of the graphical annoyances and overall making character sprites look cleaner. The introduction of talksprites for the characters was long overdue, and they look suitably adorable. The music also continues to slap, so much so that I don't even mind that most of the songs are remixes of the same track. These both do a good job in immersing you in the alien world of Alternia, a world both eerily similar and shockingly different from our own, as you emerge on deerback from the ashes of Act 1's ending. 

Act 1 does feature more mature content than Act 1--and I mean A LOT more. Act 1 was only lightly raunchy (mainly in the decor for Half-Harley Manor), toning down the aggressive edginess of Homestuck into simple whimsy and fun. Act 2 embraces that edginess of its source material head on, doubling down on all the swears and blood and dirty jokes that were all over Homestuck. I'm not saying this is inherently bad, to be clear. But it was definitely a marked contrast from Act 1, and I personally found it to be unwelcome. 

While Act 1 refined what I consider to be Homestuck's best elements into a full game format, Act 2 reminds me mostly of the Meenah games from Homestuck Act 6. Long-winded, tiring quests to get to know some of the most unlikable teenagers in all of fiction, many of whom had very little plot relevance. Hiveswap Act 2 introduces a LOT of new characters, some of whom are charming in the same manner as Act 1, but many of whom are obnoxious and annoying just like...basically every Ancestor Troll from Homestuck now that I think about it. While Act 1 handled the introductions of four characters (and did so pretty well), Act 2 tries to shove literal dozens of troll teenagers into the narrative. This would be an ambitious task for any writer, and while Act 2 could certainly do worse in this regard, it really doesn't enhance the narrative to have so many douchebags clogging up this train. 

I realize that Hiveswap:Friendsim likely fleshes these characters out more, but I don't think that's a valid excuse. I shouldn't have to play an entirely separate side game just to understand who tf anybody is. Plus, the quality of the characterization in Act 2 does not convince me that playing Friendsim would be anything other than a painful experience. As someone who appreciated how accessible Hiveswap Act 1 was, I can't help but feel disappointed that Act 2 relapsed into the Homestuck trap of requiring an insane level of immersion and investment to truly enjoy the story. 

Another thing that the number of characters makes tiring is the typing quirks. I'm sorry, I just don't get why these are still here. They were annoying enough in Homestuck, where walls of text became quickly unreadable when certain typing quirks were paired together, but they are an even bigger headache here. Some are cute, like the guy who goes -_- all the time, but most of them just make the already difficult dialogue even harder to parse. It's hard to keep any character's typing quirk distinct when there are so many of them. 

It may feel like I'm really harping on the characters, but that's because 90% of this game is about the characters! The puzzles for most of the runtime are just "wander around in the train for 5 hours talking to everybody". The concept of moving through each car of a segregated train and gradually learning about the class distinctions and problems of Alternian society is an interesting one. But in practice, the hook of "you need to get to the front or the portal is gonna blow up" makes the player consider their adventures in the train as mere detours, and wants to get them over with as soon as possible. This isn't always a big deal, as most of the train cars aren't too long. 

But then there's the tealblood car. Oh god, the tealblood car. Of my five hour play time, about three of those were spent in this goddamn car. While the idea of a trial is initially cool, and I like the pheonix wright references, it just goes on for way WAY too long. Everyone in the train car, including the defendant, thinks this trial is a waste of time. We, the player, think it's a waste of time because we just want to get moving to the end of the train. Nearly everyone in the car is an unlikable douchebag, and I brute-forced my way through the trial just so I wouldn't have to talk to them anymore. This whole sequence is just awful. It could have been better if Joey or Xefros was the defendant, and it frankly makes sense that the lowbloods would get the blame regardless of the crime. It would be nice if the trial was something more exciting than a book theft, too. This whole sequence needed...something! Something to make it feel more like a game and less like pulling teeth. 

I could go on, but I feel like I've said my piece. This whole Act just reeks of missed potential and misplaced effort. If the effort from the trial sequence had gone into another Strife (since there's only one in this act, and it's basically a fake-out), or in fleshing out the other lackluster sections, I feel like the whole experience would be vastly improved. While some parts I enjoyed, I really don't want to play this game again. I'm unlikely to buy Act 3 either, in however many decades it takes till that comes out. 

If you enjoyed it, and you think I'm a dumb poopy farthead for daring to dislike this game...okay. Enjoy what you enjoy. But for myself, I'm done with Andrew Hussie's work. No more trolls for me, thanks.

TLDR: The plot is disappointing. If you want long bricks of text about the world of the Trolls of Homestuck, a bunch of fetch quests, and nothing of import to happen, then this is the game for you. The art and music are on the whole good as usual - buy the soundtrack!

Minor over-arching spoilers for the game to follow, nothing specific:

Hiveswap: Act 1 was a very engaging story that happened to take place in the Homestuck universe. As someone who was not a fan of Homestuck, it was still easy to get into, exciting, and well written, while providing enough references to the source material to merit fans of the franchise playing it.

Hiveswap: Act 2 sees you delve deep into various aspects of the world of Homestuck, while exactly nothing happens from a plot perspective. In a grand synopsis of what will ultimately become the entire Hiveswap plot, you could sum up the entirety of Act 2 with "they tried to reach a destination." The game has some enjoyable moments, but leaves so much to be desired from a greater story perspective and leans so heavily into bricks of lore text and fetch quests that it ultimately felt meaningless. The game that took literal years of development hell to release resulted in the player and the protagonists accomplishing almost nothing. I'm left very disappointed in this after my very high hopes coming off of Act 1.

Cutscenes were well animated though their technical implementation left much to be desired (very jittery transitions, weird fades, generally jank). Background art and character art was on the whole superb as the art team is very talented, music is by and large great though due to the majority of the game taking place in one setting with musical remixes in each sub-area it did get a bit samey at times.

Paying $15 for each 5 hour bit of this supposed 8-part opus feels less and less enticing as each part takes years to develop and their plot progress gets smaller with each passing act. Very worrying trend.

Finally, the loss of the certain staff members at What Pumpkin can be felt throughout this game. While the larger elements of the plot might not have been within the purview of this writing team, the character writing is noticeably weaker than in Act 1 (where it shined). A lot of the nuance in Joey and Xefros's characters, both in their chemistry as a duo and in their own stories, was lost in this game. Xefros went from an optimistic but abused character who had a lot to work through, to a nihilist whose long "haha everything sucks lol xd" rants serve to further inject tons and tons of Alternia lore at the player, instead of being in service of his own character. That one example feels generally emblematic of a lot of the writing in this game. It's really, really unfortunate. Hopefully the team can take feedback from this game and make a game that stands on its own merits with its own story, and not one that just revels in being part of Homestuck.

First things first, this is *not* a point & click game, it's a visual novel (and not a good one). I bought this without paying much attention to reviews because I thoroughly enjoyed the first game. I won't be making that mistake again. They're nothing alike.

Pros:
- Great music. I loved how well it suited the different areas you were in. This is definitely the game's biggest strength.
- Good graphics
- Trying to use Byers the pigeon with various things continues to be entertaining

Cons:
- For the most part it lacks the humour or the first game
- A huge number of achievements that require repeated playthroughs despite adding no value
- Early decisions lock you out of some later achievements
- There's an achievement that *requires* an autoclicker
- The vast majority of the game involves talking to characters; there's very little interaction with the environment or your inventory.
- There's a huge amount of reading in the game, and an equally large number of text/reading related issues:
- Poor font choice. They've used a font with serifs. Serifs improve reading on books/newspapers/etc, but hamper it when reading on a screen. Sans serif fonts should be used for this purpose. I found it very tiring to read.
- For some reason different characters have different ways the text is displayed. Some of this attempts to reflect the way they speak, but many do not. For example, one character uses / instead of l. Anoth3r charact3r's dialogu3 is writt3n lik3 this for appar3nt no r3ason. These changes consistently make reading more tiring and frustrating.
- I found a lot of the dialogue boring, repetitive, or pointless
- A huge amount of infuriating back and forth travel.
- A lot of the 'puzzles' simply involved figuring out which of the dozens of characters on the train can/will advance the story. Once you find the character that's helpful, start at the top and talk to everyone again.
- A lot of trial and error, which can be annoying. This is made worse by a huge number of bad endings that almost seem to discourage trial and error despite it frequently being the only option.
- Due to the above, the best way to play the game is pretty much just to keep using the hint button and doing what it says
- Most of the train section felt like filler. This is a problem considering it makes up about 80% of the game. It should have been a single puzzle in a larger story.
- What passes for story really isn't very interesting, and largely fails to evoke emotion
- Xerfros's constant self deprecation 'I'm an idiot' comments get tired very quickly

Verdict: 2/10

I hate to give this long awaited sequel a negative review, but it's what I think the game deserves. So what did this game do right and what did it do wrong?

Positives: 
- The setting is honestly amazing, the segregated train cars all have a lot of personality and are a great way to involve many different kinds of trolls and show the social imbalance between the castes.
- Music and art are both excellent, the game has a very charming aesthetic. The character animations are especially great... when they aren't extremely choppy.

Negatives:
- As mentioned above, some animations look strangely unfinished, which was a problem with the first game as well. Both characters idle sprites look like they are about 5 frames per second and I don't understand why such a used animation would be cut down to such a bare minimum. 
- A couple other small nitpicks bothered me throughout the playthrough, such as not being able to examine the items in your inventory. You start the game with items from the last act and the icons for them are too small to really tell what some of them are. I went through the whole game without knowing what the book in Xefros' inventory was. The hint system can also be pretty useless at many times as well. Rather than giving you a hint it usually just repeats what your current objective is, more like a quest log than any sort of hint.
- Much of the games 'puzzles' are unintuitive and unsatisfying to solve. In the second half of the game especially I found a guide necessary for me to advance without having to repeatedly interact with everything over and over again. This makes me question why Hiveswap even had to be a game in the first place when, in my opinion, nothing is being accomplished here that couldn't have been in the webcomic format we are more used to. Or even in the style of Friendsim/Pesterquest! Those games were mostly able to maintain the strengths of Hiveswap (the music, writing, and character art) while avoiding its weaknesses (having to waste time interacting with things repeatedly to see what you're supposed to do or just look up a guide). I for one wouldn't mind making the game more linear if it meant cutting out the annoying bits.
- It feels like almost nothing has happened in Hiveswap act 1 or 2! I could sum up all of the relevant events from both games in just a couple sentences. The 'plot' is progressing at such a slow pace that I wonder how act 3 could pick up the pace and resolve everything in a satisfying way.
- I also don't really know who this game is supposed to be for? Troll romance is explained to the player through Xefros for what would be the third time for someone who has read Homestuck and played Friendsim. You would think that would mean its intended for people who haven't read the comic, but I can't imagine recommending this game to someone that hasn't already read Homestuck, or at the very least Friendsim. The best part of the game was honestly just being able to see my favorite characters from Friendsim, and the only other thing that I'm holding out for in this series is how it will relate back to Homestuck. Like, remember those black and green monsters from Hiveswap act 1? Yeah whats up with those, we still have no clue at all what their deal is. So yeah, I'm not sure who the target audience really is here, it seems more like they're trying to appeal to both but not doing a great job at it.

In conclusion:
I dunno, I feel like most people already knew if they were going to get this game before it came out. I'm personally not going to recommend this game to my friends, neither those who have read Homestuck nor those who have not read it. The game often had unsatisfying solutions, some general lack of UI and polish, and didn't really answer any new questions or contribute to the Homestuck lore.

This took an utterly ridiculous amount of time to release, especially considering how overly funded it was. A variety of problems seemingly hindered its release but in the end; this simple point and click game took three years to produce. With over two million dollars in funding that is completely unacceptable behaviour. In nearly every sense, a failure.

The game itself has a very distinct arch of quality. To start the scene transitions are extremely abrupt, multiple beginning areas feel shallow and clearly exist as a desperate reference to Friendsim, characters lack a variety of idle expressions needed to actually telegraph their mood in conversation, the inventory is overly cluttered and full of uninteresting objects that aren't very compelling to use on anything; there is also an asinine delay between when a conversation begin and actual dialogue starts being typed out. This game took three years to make.

Despite all this the start of the game does gradually build a solid atmosphere with nice pacing and decently interesting item puzzles. It really does start to replicate the quality set forth by the first act.

Then the [spoiler]trial[/spoiler] sequence begins. It is extremely long, probably over an hour long if not more, and has no direct relevance to the main story at all. From a writing perspective it is an entire derailment of the story because for probably over an hour players are basically stuck in what is practically an entirely different game with an entirely different plot; for no reason. It's like the developers randomly got bored of working on a point and click adventure game and instead decided to make this spinoff game instead. But instead of it being a spinoff they just forcibly adapted it into being a sequence in this game. 

Beyond that, from a gameplay point of view this section of the game is abhorrently unfun. The game takes what is a relatively dynamic, complicated situation and forcibly converts it into a very linear choose-the-right-dialogue-or-item-option-to-progress trial and error gauntlet that makes almost no sense over half the time. The entire sequence is meant to be about deduction and logic but it often operates under information that players simply do not know, and then the game acts like the player made a mistake for not choosing the right option. In a situation where the necessary information is either being withheld from them or buried beneath unintuitive allusions. It's like playing connect the dots with invisible dots, make a connection between two random points and hope it's correct.

This sequence is so extremely out of place, overly long, mechanically ramshackle, and entirely irrelevant to the story that it completely sapped my will to even keep playing. Because after all that, all of that, players may not even be able to select the proper conclusion in-game even if they know the final answer because the player didn't have the right items. Apparently the items that players got up until that point, from their random choices in previous parts of the game and possibly even in the first game too since the save files do transfer over; these items actually determine the players ability to reach the successful conclusion in this completely different bit of the game.

Even more absurd; the game has the audacity to give players a summary of all the things they did wrong that led to them not canonically reaching the correct conclusion. After this totally incoherent, trial and error, over an hour long sequence of badly telegraphed information driven gameplay the game lectures the player about their so-called mistakes. All this really accomplishes is further alienating players from the game by exposing how totally asinine and wasted this time was, because the conclusion was determined entirely by picking random options without proper information and or having specific random items already beforehand; not actual genuine player input. So not only was this whole thing irrelevant to the story but it also bashes whatever investment the player may have in this sequence by proving that the whole thing was out of the players control from the start.

It seems that after finishing this section of the game the developers themselves were tired too, as after that sequence the game immediately devolves into fetch quests. Over, and over, the game demands players walk back and forth along a very long horizontal map talking to characters to perform multiple fetch quests. Talk to character, walk down one side of the map, pick up item, go back, talk to character, progress, talk to new character, repeat. The game does this perhaps seven times in a row; this is the entire remainder of the experience before the final puzzle. The game even acknowledges that it's giving players fetch quests in a funny bit of dialogue as some kind of twisted irony that it is self aware of its own lazy, shallow design. They took three years with this and still skimped out on the entire second half of the game after also skimping out on multiple starting areas.

The final puzzle is a complete mess of asinine, random trial and error use-random-items-on-random-things over and over until something happens gauntlet as well. Players can also be game over'd by certain decisions and forced to go through the whole process again for no reason. Players aren't even allowed to save during this part, the game literally stops acknowledging saves, completely forcing players to be reset if they get a spontaneous game over from a random item interaction.

And as nice as it is to see all the trolls from the Friendsim game in this one, it also is extremely awkward that somehow they all magically ended up appearing in the story. Not even spread out, they almost all show up in this act in one massive reference dump inexplicably. And players almost exclusively only interact with them, all the other new trolls are just background decoration. Except for maybe three. I believe at least one of them is the troll that some one paid the creator large amounts of money to be able to design their own troll and have it put in the game. Because apparently the creator has no respect for their own work and is willing to sell canonical access to money hoarders who can afford to dump thousands if not tens of thousands of dollars into an indie game kickstarter to reach exclusive backer tiers. Ironic corruption considering that the story of Alternia is all about corruption and inequality.


In spite of all the aforementioned smaller problems the game has, which are especially disturbing considering how long the developers had to work on it and smooth these things out for a proper release, the first couple hours of the game are genuinely fun and live fairly well up to the quality the first game set. But the mid game sequence was draining, erroneous to the plot, frustrating, confusing and ultimately invalidates itself by revealing that from the start the player was doomed to the conclusion they'll reach by not having the right items already or picking the right random dialogue options. Then after that huge exhausting waste of time, the story resumes to now suddenly just be a bunch of awful fetch quests purposely stringing the player along pointless distances for zero reason besides desperate padding. And to top it all off; the final puzzle is an incoherent trial and error gauntlet of absolutely asinine item usages. 

A strong, promising start and ascent; followed by a baffling, absurd intermission; then by a shallow decline straight into a frustrating and unsatisfying conclusion.

Hiveswap: Act 2 is a game riddled with bugs, detrimental shortcuts, and tedious gameplay. When I first played and finished this game I was fine with it, but looking back I realize that most of my enjoyment came from the visuals and dialogue rather than any other part. The actual game part of it is downright embarrassing for a project thats been in development for almost a decade now.

The main gameplay is basically the same as the first act of Hiveswap. It works fine and I don't have any complaints about how it's laid out. What I DO have a problem with is the inane bullshittery that is the puzzles. You can barely apply logic to most of these puzzles, they're that bad. It either comes down to using every single item you have on every single object in the room or talking to every single character in the room again even if it seems like they dont have anything else to say. You cannot make it through this game on your own without using hints, because nothing you do makes any sense. The trial portion of the game shares similar problems, with the evidence needed to progress often not being clear. The worst part of the game however is definitely the final portion. It is quite literally nothing but backtracking over and over again. You have to go down the map about six different times during this section, and there's no way to quickly get to a location. As someone who really enjoyed the first act of Hiveswap, I gotta say that I was really disappointed with this one, especially with how long it took to come out after Act 1. A large portion of this game takes place on a train with multiple cars, segregated by blood spectrum. You travel between the cars trying to reach the front in order to switch train-tracks to get on the fast track to reach a party in time before its too late, that way you can get the info necessary to head back home. 

Unfortunately, the game really slogs down after a few carts in, and you do have to go back through the cars MULTIPLE times to accomplish objectives, and there's no fast-travel map of the train, so that means you have to go through multiple loading screens going through not only each car, but each section CONNECTING each car. Its something that would've been so simple to incorporate, but it wasn't, which adds a lot of unnecessary padding to this game's run time. There was also a section where I thought I could perform a little side quest as I was going through each train car in order to help out one of the troll's who had a sick/injured lusus, which I was excited to complete, but there was no point at any time where I could've gotten what I needed to help that troll before I reached the ending. I won't spoil the ending by the way, but it also wasn't worth all the extra fluff in between all the train cars leading up to it. 

Everything I did felt pointless at the end of it, as none of it really mattered. Three years of wait on this game and it most certainly was not worth the wait when compared to how much better the first game was compared to this one. No amount of Hiveswap Friendsim characters they threw in can make this game more worth it than it is. Don't pick it up for its initial $14.99 asking price, wait for it to drop or go on sale before you buy it if you want to continue the Hiveswap series. The first one is much better, and its only asking for $7.99 right now. I just hope act 3 doesn't take too long and we can continue the adventure, and hopefully it'll be a better entry in the series than this one is.

Wow. It took them years to release the second act and it's somehow worse than the first. Where do I even begin?

-The art is nice
-Some of the jokes are kind of funny
-The music is amazing, but considering it's Homestuck, that's kind of a given

Okay, now onto the bad things...
First of all, this game's animation is nowhere near as good as the first act. There are NO animated cutscenes like in the first act for some reason, character movement and perspectives can look wonky and jarring (examples: The main character getting up in a scene, it does a freaking fade in fade out transition instead of animating it, and the characters walking on a bridge has weird perspective problems.) Yeah, it just doesn't move as nicely.

Second, I got a glitch that made the game completely unplayable. There's a part where you need to get train tickets so you can board the train, and I got the tickets, but it just wouldn't let me get on the train. Like, there was no option to be able to do so. The only thing I could do was start the whole game over again, and screw that! Luckily, the glitch happened on my second playthrough.

Third, this game is a slog to get through. A lot of the "gameplay" is just wandering around and reading useless flavour text, and this is coming from someone who loves point-and-click adventure games! The problem is that the dialogue just isn't that funny or memorable. Similar games like, say, The Curse of Monkey Island (I'm using the third game as a comparison because it's my favourite) has so many funny jokes and memorable lines, so it's not boring or tedious to go through dialogue trees or interact with useless items. This game (Hiveswap act 2) does not succeed in investing me in it's story, and I played this when I was still into Homestuck.

And finally, fourth. The characters aren't likeable. None of them. And the ones I didn't dislike were just boring and forgettable. It's extremely, painfully clearly unpolished. Like they tried to meet some imaginary deadline. I'll try to explain my best.

[b] Firstly, the plot/the gameplay [/b]
The part of the game prior to the train is visibly lacking momentum and has problems with pacing.
Spoilers ahead I guess, but honestly it's not much.
You go from one station, to the mountain, to the cave, to the Zebede's hive, to another station in the span of 10 minutes (maybe a bit more if you get stuck on simplistic puzzles). That part feels weirdly lonely, and honestly it's obvious what's wrong if you rewatch the trailer that was posted back at the end of October: there's no Charun! For some freakin reason they cut out Charun (and most likely Zebede too) from the game just a month before release? Without them the cave and Zebede's hive feel just wrong. It feels like they wouldn've been such an important piece of the plot, and they were just ditched. I'm lost on this

The train is okay. Not really great in terms of puzzles (except the engine car), and it forces you to do A LOT of walking from one end to another, which got just a bit old at the end. The courtroom part dragged on forever, and instead of being the cornerstone of Act 2 (which what I presume Pumpkins were hoping for), it was just.. kind of a slog? Like, it's such a sudden change of pace, I personally wasn't prepared to play Act Attorney at all.

[b] Da writing [/b]
Personally, while the writing was plentiful: like, damn, this was more a visual novel than a puzzle game, but I guess I wouldn't mind if the writing was.. better? Honestly, I can't tell it's bad, because it's really not, but something felt off to me. It just didn't hit me like it did in Act 1. But you get to interact with the trollcall cast and receive some worldbuilding titbits, which is appreciated. But still, I felt like the writing was more cut-and-dried. Funky item interactions were stripped down in favor of more general responses, and there were a lot LESS stuff to click on in general. 

[b] Now, the art [/b]
I must say, the backgrounds are still beatiful, just like in Act 1, whoever was responsible for the art really did their best, it felt almost immersive. Unofrtunately, this amazing artwork is just that - a background. Again, you can't interact with a lot of stuff. 
The thing I have gripe the most with are transitions. Transitions from one place to another really killed the pace, because there simply were none. For exmaple, when you get yourself the tickets and decide to board the train, you click on the gate, and with no visual representation whatsoever, appear in the lowblood car. Like, Act 1 had all those beautiful transitions (even the smallest stuff like Joey using the green cube thingy in Dammek's hive), which really set the mood, whereas in Act 2.. you get none of that. The most we see is one frame of an explosion and clunky game over screens. It's as if they didn't have the time to make all of it

[b] Now, the music. [/b]
Well, ugh, there really weren't a lot of it. At least, this is what it felt like to me. Like, I think that variations playing in different cars slapped for sure, but I can't remember a single other track from Act 2. I really would like to mention a video, which James Roach posted a long time ago on youtube (which is now deleted??), where he showed variating themes for trolls of different castes. They were supposed to play when you'd TALK to a troll, but, obviously, we didn't get that at the end, sadly. 
Additionally, I'd like to point out the laziest reuse of a track from the Act 1 (the "Old secret" one), in the closing scene. Personally, it felt like it didn't fit the scene at all, and honestly I'm just surprised they couldn't write another track. 


My overall play time was almost 10 hours, which is a lot more than Act 1, but at least the third of that time must've been spent in the teal car, which isn't a good sign. 


Overall, I honestly believe that we have gotten a half-baked game made in 2 or 3 months. I heard this is somehow the fault of viz, but if this is true, it's the second time What Pumpkins have been played by some other company, and at this point I don't know what to make of it.
 I don't really regret spending my money (that's not my problem with it). Rather, I feel like the second installment of the game I was anticipating for a long time kind of disappointed me. I really got a lot more enjoyment out of replaying Act 1 like 3 times to get all the achievements, to hang out in all the different locations and see all the writing. with which that game filled to the brim. This... this is just heartbreaking, honestly. I'm really scared of what will come next. If it will come at all.

I LOVED each of these characters, even though (and probably because) I never played any of the Friendsim spinoffs and only heartell of their exploits or flaws from other obsessed fangirls.  All of the background characters have animations too, from the paranoid to the relaxed or jovial!  Of all the little quirks and features, Zebruh's walk animation is definitely my favorite thing in the whole game, it's just... such a pleasure.  They'll probably be the only thing keeping you in the game.

Each of these alien characters is very charming, likable or... engaging at some level, and the game makes sure you spend as much time with each one as possible.  That's why half of the achievements require six hours of backtracking to undo a minor choice early on so a different particular character shows up later.  And they're all mutually exclusive.  Seriously.  You have to play through the whole 10-hour game a minimum of four times to get all the achievements.  Not even Black Mesa was this cruel!

People have complained about how there is no "dialogue backspace" button and it makes it difficult to remember or comprehend certain story elements if you weren't listening, but that adds to the realism and I greatly enjoyed it!  They don't just repeat the same things over and over like a robot, they'll say something else as if it were a real conversation and they're not gonna repeat themselves.  This also shows the sheer depth of the writing scale as each character has new things to say with each story beat!  Don't worry about missing info; if you want all the achievements in the game, you're going to be rereading the same dialogue several times anyway.

As for bugs, the only ones I encountered were cutscene glitches which served to heighten the atmosphere of terror in the later stages of the game involving... well I'd rather not say.  Let's just say it gets disturbing and the alien companion's fears are justified.  But I digress!  Act 1 was bug-ridden garbage, the bugs in Act 2 are minimal.  This is probably because they cut all the minigames, which was the worst part of Act 1 by a longshot.

As for the quality of the writing itself, it's still a far cry from Hussie's rapier wit, but it's not the Cohenist veganism either.  There's some preachy segments about classism or halfhearted sentiments about challenging the system through rap, but it doesn't go anywhere and wasn't nearly as heavy-handed as the Peta-esque nonsense from the last game that they thought passed as dialogue.  The dialogue in this game is a lot cleaner and less awkward, and does a great job handling large amounts of characters.  

It's everything it promised to be.  Either that, or my expectations got so low I forgot what I paid for.

They make you spend 2 hours in a drawn out Ace Attorney parody.

It... it's awful.  This game is awful.  There are so many better point-and-clicks on the market with actual clever writing you could be spending your time and money on (got this in a bundle so I have an excuse).

You are all way too forgiving.

HIVESWAP is a hand-drawn point & click adventure game where you play as Joey Claire, a puzzle-solving teen snatched out of the comfort of her own home and left stranded on a hostile alien planet on the brink of a rebellion. In ACT 2, you continue on your journey with the troll named Xefros, trying to find your way to a party held by a friend of his moirail, Dammek. You get to meet dozens of unique and memorable characters, some of which are more helpful than others, as you navigate through this volatile alien culture.

Most of the game in act 2 is happening on a train ride to the party. You have to go through different train carriages that hold different trolls of the Hemospectrum, the Rust and Bronze bloods, the Gold and Olive bloods, the Jade and Teal bloods, the Blue and Indigo bloods and the Purple bloods. Each carriage gives you different puzzles/quests to solve and how to move forward in your journey to the front of the train.

In my honest opinion, this act was quite good and didn't leave me unhappy. I played through act 1 and act 2 almost back to back, and I noticed a lot of differences. Where act 1 was more of an actual point & click, with puzzles to solve and items to interact with, act 2 gives you more of a dialogue based game that reminds you of a visual novel. There is almost no point & click puzzles to solve, until near the end, and most of the problems you need to figure out is by talking to multiple characters.

On the positive side, the more dialogue based gameplay can be very impressive, since as you progress you find more new characters who have many different things to say to you, each time you talk to them. Every one of them weighs in, helpfully or not, on every part of every puzzle. Huge amounts of dialogue to be read.

On the flip side however, this more dialogue based gameplay can end up quite brainless and boring, as you keep talking to characters over and over and over again. Some people might like that, but many will not find it fun.

In the end, the amount waited for this act, and the fact that they strayed farther away from the point & click aspect, I don't think I can recommend this part of the game. I did enjoy it, and there were lots of twists that I didn't see them coming, but it's just isn't worth it. Considering also that you'll probably have to wait for the next chapter... forever. I am not unhappy with the game, I just can't recommend it forwards.

What remains of Hiveswap is a rather lifeless journey through a series of beautifully crafted dioramas of lovingly animated trolls that all have increasingly bizarre yet charming personalities; what's clear with Act 2 is a devotion to character writing, as is common with post-Act 7 Homestuck content, with little effort placed into actual world building. TL;DR This honestly would have been a more enjoyable experience if it was a VN like Friendsim.

Act 2 plays and feels like a product of significantly lower quality than Act 1. 
In short, it hardly feels like a sequel at all, at least in regards to gameplay. Act 1 was a pleasant surprise following its tumultuous conception and development. Charming and well polished, it gave me high hopes for the next in the series. That was a long wait, and unfortunately I can't rightly say Act 2 lived up to my hopes.

As I understand it, the original team that worked on Act 1 was majorly laid off after Viz acquired Homestuck. I was hoping this wouldn't result in too much turbulence when it came to continuing the Hiveswap series, but going from the first act to this game gave me whiplash. 

This game is presented as the sequel to Hiveswap: Act 1, obviously, but it plays more like a sequel to Hiveswap: Friendsim (The 0.99$ VN's that were released episodically after Act 1, and before this game).

Instead of playing like a point and click adventure game, like the previous game, [b]this plays a lot more like a VN[/b]. 

You retain your inventory from the first game if you carry your save over, but for the VAST majority of the game you don't use anything and you spend most of your time going through dialogues with characters from Friendsim. Each screen from the first game had plenty of objects that you could interact with in different ways with your items and abilities; In this game, there are hardly any items in the background to find or do anything with, and it makes them feel much hollower. You only interact with characters for the most part, and most screens consist of walking back and forth between characters until you exhaust their dialogue and the game lets you proceed to the next screen. 

Some of the longer sections of the game are just long because you have to walk all the way from the front of the train to the back, and then to the front again. At one point you have to walk from the VERY FRONT all the way to the back, just to have your character say "Well I didn't need to do this" and have you walk all the way up to the front again. And strangely enough, the walking mechanics are... spotty? You have to mash click to keep moving, and sometimes you will just... stop. It's a weird thing to mention but... This is the "core gameplay". so it's worth mentioning.

There are two significant sections of the game that I would say actually constitute "puzzles"; The trial, and the finale in the front car. Keep in mind this game is [i]very[/i] short. I think your mileage will vary when it comes to these; Personally, I did not think either event was very good by adventure game standards.

[spoiler]The outcome of the trial is apparently decided by an unrelated dialogue from an unrelated character BEFORE you board the train; If you don't select a certain option, you will not be able to access the "Good" ending to the trial. I'm not a big fan of that. The trial itself isn't exactly going to be putting Phoenix Wright out of business anyway. As mentioned below, keeping track of your items and the timeline in the trial is inconsistent and un-intuitive.[/spoiler]

The game falls short of Act 1 in other departments as well:
There is a real inconsistency to the quality of the assets in the game. Some backgrounds can be very quality, but others will have very obvious artifacting, or just be way lower resolution. 
Example: Moving from the indigo car to the purple car. The indigo background is very nice and high quality, but the transition between the cars and the purple car are much lower resolution, and some places have very harsh artifacting present.
One of the worst and most obvious discrepancies in quality is in the final sequence; Using Byers in the final sequence releases him and he has a flying animation, but when he lands again his sprite reverts to an asset from the previous game... But it's not properly cut out. The sprite is surrounded by a spotty white pixel halo from it not being prepared properly for transparency. This is very confusing because it's very obvious, and I'm pretty sure nearly anyone could fix this problem in under an hour in photoshop.
These are just some specific examples, these kind of discrepancies are present mostly throughout the length of the game.

There's also small general inconsistencies in miscellaneous areas of the game;
- Some items you acquire (Namely for the trial) go into your inventory, but some don't for whatever reason. It can be hard to keep track of what you actually have, because you can't even check the trial timeline/suspects/etc. until actually starting the trial. Sometimes you can't even check the timeline while questioning a witness, which is very annoying.
- Your interactions are commonly inconsistent: Some doors you just walk through by clicking, some open a little Look/Exit menu and you have to click again. 
- Some characters will talk very slowly, which makes me want to click to fill out their text box so I can read it. But when you are in a dialogue with multiple characters, sometimes one can speak VERY QUICKLY, which will cause you to skip over their text if you're in a rythm. The VNs avoid this problem by letting you go back through dialogue... And again, this basically plays like a VN. 

These are clearly very small criticisms, but you have to remember that these are basically the mechanics of the whole game. It gets annoying over time. The VNs were 90 cents, and also focused on dialogue... And they don't suffer from the same QoL problems.
You feel the minor annoyances a lot more because there's just not a lot else going on.

This is a very nitpicky example to mention, but even the achievements are arguably lower quality. The first game has unique little icons for each achievement, but this game uses the same icon for all of them. It might not mean much but to me it does illustrate a difference in the level of care this time around. 

I hate to say it, but this episode makes it harder to recommend Act 1, which is already a pretty niche title. I hope that the next installment makes some improvements, or at least reclaims some of the good aspects of the first game.

PS. The achievement for continuing your save still hasn't unlocked for me, which is really annoying me.

My final recomendation is: Don't play if you're not a Homestuck fan. If you are a Homestuck fan: Don't be afraid to consult a guide or use the hint system if you ever start feeling a little frustrated- trying to figure certain parts out does NOT feel rewarding when the solution is simply so convoluted only the developers know what it is.

While it's a bumpy ride to say the least, Hiveswap Act 2 is where I feel that the Hiveswap series finally finds its footing. Act 1 was a nice novelty and Friendsim was a mixed bag with highs and lows, so it was nice to feel an actually solid entry that feels worth getting to for Homestuck fans.

The first few sections play similar to Act 1 where you progress through the game in typical point & click fashion and just comes across as alright. However it's around halfway through the train that you reach one of the major sections, featuring the teal and jade caste who also so happen to have the most interesting characters from Friendsim. The bulk of Act 2 is spent in a trial where the player has to try to put together evidence, and this is certainly the most mixed bag section... the trial itself wasn't the best put together as it's hard to reach logical conclusions on our own like an actual puzzle, however engaging with each character and exploring different dialogue trees did have me invested to the end.

The train car after the trial is the lowpoint of the game for me, it just drags on. While there's a few interesting moments, it  loses the momentum for me that the trial was building and I sort of wish it was just.. skipped. Luckily the game comes back around in the end to really raise the stakes in an interesting way, making me looking forward to Act 3.

But please... do better by your developers and fans alike. There are a lot of decisions still being made that clearly does not have the game's best interests in mind.

- the interactions between the two main protagonists was by far my favorite part of the game: their dynamic is enjoyable to read and i love reading the conversations they have. it's very wholesome, and it's one of the places where the game really shines. the art is beautiful as well, and i got really excited at seeing all of the cute reactions and expressions everyone has. i know this is only one bullet point, but i have a glowing adoration for both of these elements of the game, and i had a lot of fun moving through the world because of them.

- following that, i also really enjoyed the story, though i admit that is entirely personal preference and i have seen opinions that differed. during the last part of the game especially, without spoilers, i was tense and excited and really interested to see how things would play out.

- the gameplay is rather weak at times: there's a lot of backtracking in the latter half of the game and a lot of players have expressed frustration with the puzzles. the game does not often provide any meaningful guidance that would allow you to think through things yourselves. it usually comes down to a lot of tedious trial-and-error, and i personally never felt very rewarded when i did get a puzzle right.

- there is a part of the game that is an extended ace attorney parody, and it is by far the worst part of the game, story and gameplay wise. the logic and answers are extremely convoluted, and the segment overstays its welcome tenfold. it actively drains the rest of the game's experience and is an enormous black mark on a game that could otherwise be viewed favorably.

- i enjoyed the myriad ways the game can branch off, and i think it's interesting to think about how those may affect future acts. i really love achievement hunting and replaying games, which was a significant draw towards act 2, but the AA part of the game makes that concept far more frustrating, which goes to show how the worst parts of this game brings down the product as a whole.

i would recommend this game if you like homestuck and enjoy the troll call cast, though i would hesitate to extend that same welcome to any wider audience. a lot of people have had very different experiences playing this game! i had fun and i think it's possible for a lot of people to have fun too. it's a decision you need to make for yourself.

lastly, and i think this is probably the [b]most important[/b] part, and would be a mistake if it were left out of any review:

fans have had to wait for this game for three years, and to be frank, it is rather buggy at times and feels as if it's been cobbled together and rushed at many points. it has had a complicated development lifecycle involving a lot of bad luck, bad decisions, endless delays, and a lack of transparency, which makes it really hard to trust the developers. furthermore, and this might honestly be one of the worst parts of the game: there is no credits page. none. none of the people who worked on this game are given any sort of acknowledgement for their hard work, which is not only horrible to the contributors, but extremely suspicious. i couldn't truly say why nobody is credited (their response as to why is rather unsatisfying), or why the game has taken so long for a product that is rather disappointing, but something messed up is going on in this game and behind the scenes, and i think that should be considered before you give them your money.

[b]edit:[/b] credits have since been added, but their reasoning for not doing so upon launch is extremely flimsy and it's almost certain they lied in their response addressing the situation. i cannot verify if the credits include all of those who have previously made assets for the game but are no longer on the team, but at least some of them are, and further speculation should not really be on a steam review. consider that issue remedied, at least in part

[h1]After waiting over 3 years for Act 2 to be released, I can sadly say that it was not worth the wait.[/h1] The effects of development hell are pretty apparent as there is obvious cut content in the early sections of the game. Promised characters like Charun and Zebede are completely absent despite being shown in the now deleted announcement trailer back from 2019. Hell, in Zebede's case, an entire mini-game was just cut because players found it too hard and is now only accessible to Day 1 players. Also, Act 1 featured fully animated cutscenes, while Act 2 only has animatics. For those not familiar with the term, not of the cutscenes are actually animated, they simply cut from frame to frame and this is usually used as a storyboarding technique. The use of a shortcut technique to avoid time on animation and the cut content really tells that the painfully delayed product was actually rushed despite the 3 year time period they had.

That's not even factoring that the finished product is very underwhelming on its own. The vastly detailed and cruelly engaging world of Alternia is limited to just a train for three-quarters of the game. When I think of an alien world to explore, I'd want to city the towns, cities, caves, forests, deserts, or one of a kind biomes that I would never see on Earth. The train route also makes the gameplay and area progression a literal straight line. The problems with the game's map layout becomes even more apparent when the final section of the game has you do backtracking. Like, a lot of backtracking. I know it's a point and click game and that already limits what you can do with the gameplay, but please do something over than fetchquests. Oh, and if I wanted to play a Phoenix Wright game, I'd play a Phoenix Wright game. After playing through both all the Danganronpa games and the Phoenix Wright trilogy, I can safely say that the Hiveswap court case is a gigantic waste of time that you can just have the answers hand-fed to you in. It's boring and really overstays its welcome. Onto a topic I actually enjoyed, the multiple options you could take to solve some of the game's puzzles was actually really well done! It's not something along the lines of multiple endings, but I enjoy the ability of having multiple solutions to a single problem. On a final note on this incredibly short game, I hope you like the song called Ticket to Ride. Because that song and the several remixes of it will be all you hear once you step on that stupid train.

I don't think I would be nearly as bothered as I am with Act 2 if it wasn't for the terrible management choices Hussie (and to a lesser extent the WP team) made. Andrew Hussie has shown a complete lack of care for Hiveswap, yet refuses to allow other people to continue the story he has no care for. In between the release of the two acts, Hussie started 4 other projects that ate up time and resources that could've been devoted to Act 2. Even after Act 2's release, Hussie has started yet another project and left the Hiveswap team despite the original kickstarter promising 4 acts AND Hauntswitch. This combined with The Odd Gentleman leaks really gives me the impression that we'll either never get future acts or that the quality is going to take a drastic dip. For those who aren't aware of TOG leaks or how they're involved:  TOG was a studio that Hussie initially hired to work on Hiveswap but cut ties with them after they supposedly "stole funds". What seems to have actually happened was that Hussie was an abusive boss that set unrealistic goals for the dev team that could've changed on a complete whim. Projects, models, concepts, drafts, etc. would be nearly completed and Hussie would decide he's not happy with it at the very last minute. There's more to it, but I'd rather you find the initial reports on it, as I'd risk inaccuracy even further. I have chosen to believe the claims against Hussie as they would very easily explain the lack of a court case for TOG allegedly stealing crowdfunded money. 

[b]Overall, I am not happy with Act 2 because of the final product we got and because of the complete disinterest shown by the project's "head".[/b]

I didn't want to mark this as not recommended, since I did enjoy playing, a couple of jokes landed, yellow/olive and engine cars were fun, it's aesthetically pleasing, and it's still better Homestuck-related content than HS^2, but I ended up changing my mind upon trying to replay it and finding the first segment such a slog I just couldn't force myself get through it.

Firstly, writing a review for this game is extremely difficult. This act in the HIVESWAP series has a lot of good and bad attributes. Let’s start with the good. The art direction in this act is just as good as the first one, if not better. There are significantly more characters in this act than the first one. The decision to partially animate the character sprites was very clever. Partially animating the sprites helps the player keep track of which character are speaking, especially since there are numerous characters on screen at certain parts in the story, this drastically reduces confusion. That being said, the animation in this act is as good as the animation in the first act. However, the writing in this act is a mixed bag. The writing is pretty standard up until the player reaches the third train car, then the writing goes off the rails (no pun intended). The writing becomes very explicit, very quickly. Complete tonal whiplash compared to all the interactions and scenes before it. I’m not against that style of writing, but I wasn’t expecting it either, really caught me off guard. The gameplay is the same as the first act, with the exception of a few sections. The gameplay is slightly less linear than the first act, since there are alternative outcomes based off your choices. There’s more fail states in this act, so be careful. There’s a lot of unique optional character dialog throughout this act. Most character dialog changes as you progress through the story, which I found to be a really nice touch. Furthermore, this act is also composed by Toby Fox, which is just a short way of saying the music is still good, no surprise there. Now, the bad. The Ace Attorney segment that happens in the third train car is easily the worst part of the act. It feels like the developers didn’t understand why the Ace Attorney games worked mechanically. The developers knew this section of the game would be difficult and confusing for players, given the absurd amount of chances you’re granted and the generous hint system. Normally, with Ace Attorney games the player is given several statements and it’s the player’s job to spot the contradiction in one of the statements. Afterwards, the player would present “evidence” that proves the statement is a contradiction. If you are having trouble deciding which statement has a contradiction, you can “press” for more information. In rare cases, pressing statements is needed to progress the cross-examination. In this act, the contradictions in cross-examination statements aren’t always clear. Sometimes you’re not spotting a contradiction per se, just a statement you have to add more context to. If you have never played an Ace Attorney game before, you are going to struggle with that section of the game. Additionally, the writing in the third train car is very mature, explicit even. It’s like the section of the game was written by a completely different team. The whole trial in the third train car felt so surreal. I’m not entirely sure what happened during the development of that section, but it was insane. Luckily, the game returns to its normal self afterwards. Nonetheless, the section of game where Joey needs to challenge Nihkee to a theater brawl was also a little annoying. To complete that section of the game the player has to talk to Ardata, a character that will (optionally) endgame you with every interaction, after talking to Elwurd. There’s no indication that you have to talk to Ardata to progress the story. I ended up talking to Ardata and agreeing with her proposal after talking to every interactable character on the train up to that point (very risky). Then, there’s the final boss of the act. Some of the sequences are odd. For example, the player has to command Joey tap dance to shake the hula girl dashboard doll, which causes the dashboard doll to dance somehow. How does Joey generate enough force to cause this phenomenon when the moving train couldn’t? Not important. Why does a drone controlled vehicle need a dashboard doll? Doesn’t matter. Then the player has to command Joey to shine her flashlight at the dashboard doll, which causes it to shine and distract the drone. I’m not sure why the doll needs to be moving to accomplish this goal, but it’s what’s needed to solve the puzzle. The player, controlling Joey, needs to throw pet food at the train control panel, which causes Byers, the pigeon, to fly and land towards the drone. Then, the player, controlling Xefros, needs to use telekinesis to pull down the control lever. If the player uses Xefros’ telekinesis too early, it’s an immediate game over. I’m not sure why this is the case, but it needs to be done to solve the puzzle. Finally, at the time of writing this review, I am not a fan or familiar with the lore surrounding the Homestuck series. Therefore, I cannot commentate on how faithful the portrayal of certain characters are, the accuracy of the worldbuilding, or references in the game. Moreover, it’s obvious that there was a lot of work put into this act. Compared to act 1, act 2 feels lacking with all the effort put into it.

As much as I enjoyed Hiveswap: Act 1, I can't recommend Act 2. It continues the story begun in Act 1, and about 80% of it is just fine; Joey and Xephros continue their journey across Alternia, trying to find a way to get Joey back home. It's the remaining 20% that spoil it, though.

First, there's the trial scene. It involves ten or so people I whose names I couldn't keep straight, but none of whom were sympathetic. Add to that the extremely low stakes (someone stole someone's book and tore some pages out of it), and I really couldn't bring myself to give a crap about the situation. None of it concerned Joey or Xephros in any way, either; this was just something that needed to be done to get to the next bit. But even with a walkthrough, it went on for-bloody-ever.

The chapters at the end got rather weak as well: there's a problem in a lot of point-and-click puzzles where you get stuck and wind up combining every object in your inventory with every other object, in hopes of finding the magic combination that the game designer had in mind. Hiveswap isn't big on inventory puzzles, but it had something similar: with few or no clues on how to proceed, I wound up having to talk to every person in every location, to see if they were the one with the information our heroes needed.

In short, there's nothing fundamentally wrong with this game, just some lack of editing. But that's bad enough to spoil the overall experience for me.
